Animals with spots.Leopard: Each leopard's rosette pattern is unique, like a fingerprint, and helps it vanish in dappled shade.
Animals with spots.Cheetah: The cheetah's solid black spots cover a tawny coat, while the king cheetah has a rare mutation that blends them into stripes.
Animals with spots.Jaguar: Jaguar rosettes often contain a central dot, and the black form, a 'black panther', still shows ghost spots in sunlight.
Animals with spots.Dalmatian: Dalmatians are born white, and their spots appear after a few weeks; they once ran beside horse-drawn fire engines.
Animals with spots.Ladybug: A ladybug's spots don't tell its age, and those bright colours warn predators of its bitter taste.
Animals with spots.Spotted hyena: Spotted hyena females are larger and more dominant than males, and the clan's cackle is a social signal rather than laughter.
Animals with spots.Whale shark: Whale sharks have a spot pattern unique to each individual, and scientists identify them by their spots, like star maps.
Animals with spots.Fawn: Newborn deer are spotted, and the white dots help them hide on the forest floor while their mother is away.
Animals with spots.Appaloosa: Appaloosa horses are known for spotted coats, and they were bred by the Nez Perce people of the northwestern US.
Animals with spots.Leopard gecko: Leopard geckos get their name from their spots, and they store fat in their tails and can drop the tail when threatened.
Animals with spots.Ocelot: The ocelot's spotted coat was once so prized for fur that it became endangered, but protection has helped its recovery.
Animals with spots.Serval: A serval's spots help it blend into tall savanna grass, and it has the biggest ears relative to its body size of any cat.
Animals with spots.Zebra: Zebras have stripes, not spots, and every zebra's pattern is unique.
Animals with spots.Tiger: Tigers have stripes, not spots, but tiger cubs' stripes are visible even on their skin.
Animals with spots.Skunk: Skunks are black with white stripes, not spots, and the pattern warns predators.
Animals with spots.Okapi: Okapis have stripes on their legs and rump, not spots, though they are giraffe cousins.
Animals with spots.Giant panda: Giant pandas are patchy black and white, but they have no spots at all.
Animals with spots.Raccoon: Raccoons have a black mask and ringed tail, not spots, which helps them look like bandits.
Animals with spots.Lion: Lions have plain tawny coats; cubs are born with faint spots that mostly fade as they grow.
Animals with spots.Grizzly bear: Grizzly bears have no spots, and their name comes from the silver-tipped fur on their coats.
Animals with spots.Flamingo: Flamingos are uniformly pink, not spotted, and they stand on one leg to conserve body heat.
Animals with spots.Crow: Crows are glossy black without spots, and they can remember human faces for years.
Animals with spots.Chipmunk: Chipmunks have stripes along the back, not spots, and a striped face.
Animals with spots.Bumblebee: Bumblebees are fuzzy with banded stripes, not spots, and they can fly even in cool weather by shivering their flight muscles.

Plant-eating dinosaurs.Triceratops: Its frill and three horns may have been for display as much as defense, and it chewed tough plants with hundreds of teeth.
Plant-eating dinosaurs.Stegosaurus: Its plates may have helped regulate temperature or served as display, and it browsed low-growing plants.
Plant-eating dinosaurs.Brachiosaurus: It used its giraffe-like neck to browse treetops and may have eaten hundreds of kilograms of leaves each day.
Plant-eating dinosaurs.Diplodocus: One of the longest dinosaurs at about 25 meters; its pencil-like teeth stripped leaves from branches without chewing.
Plant-eating dinosaurs.Ankylosaurus: A walking tank of bony armor, it ate low plants, and its tail club could crush bone.
Plant-eating dinosaurs.Iguanodon: One of the first dinosaurs ever identified; its thumb spikes were probably for defense, while it ate plants.
Plant-eating dinosaurs.Parasaurolophus: Its hollow head crest likely worked like a horn for calls, and it chewed with batteries of grinding teeth.
Plant-eating dinosaurs.Apatosaurus: Once misnamed Brontosaurus, it was a gentle giant; the old name was revived in 2015 by some scientists.
Plant-eating dinosaurs.Argentinosaurus: One of the biggest land animals ever, possibly 70 to 100 tonnes and around 30 meters long, eating only plants.
Plant-eating dinosaurs.Edmontosaurus: A duck-billed dinosaur with a mouth packed with hundreds of teeth; some of its fossils preserve skin impressions.
Plant-eating dinosaurs.Protoceratops: A sheep-sized relative of Triceratops; one fossil famously shows it locked in battle with a Velociraptor.
Plant-eating dinosaurs.Maiasaura: Its name means good mother lizard, because fossils show it tended its nests and cared for its young.
Plant-eating dinosaurs.Tyrannosaurus: A trap: T. rex was a meat-eater, a predator with powerful jaws, not a plant eater.
Plant-eating dinosaurs.Velociraptor: A trap: it was a small feathered predator that ate meat.
Plant-eating dinosaurs.Allosaurus: A top Jurassic predator, a meat-eater with serrated teeth, and not a plant-eater.
Plant-eating dinosaurs.Spinosaurus: A trap: this giant ate fish, hunting along rivers with its crocodile-like snout.
Plant-eating dinosaurs.Giganotosaurus: A trap: it was a giant South American meat-eater, perhaps rivaling T. rex in size.
Plant-eating dinosaurs.Carnotaurus: Its name means meat-eating bull, because of its two horns above the eyes, and it hunted other animals.
Plant-eating dinosaurs.Dilophosaurus: A meat-eater with two head crests; the spitting, frilled version from Jurassic Park was invented for the film.
Plant-eating dinosaurs.Deinonychus: A trap: its name means terrible claw, and this feathered hunter's sickle claw helped inspire the raptors of the movies.
Plant-eating dinosaurs.Compsognathus: A turkey-sized meat-eater, among the smallest known dinosaurs, that ate small lizards and insects.
Plant-eating dinosaurs.Baryonyx: A trap: it had a long snout and big claws and ate fish, so it was no plant eater.
Plant-eating dinosaurs.Utahraptor: The largest known raptor, around 6 meters long, was a predator with a sickle claw.
Plant-eating dinosaurs.Albertosaurus: A trap: a smaller tyrannosaur from Canada, a meat-eater that hunted in the Cretaceous.

Animals that could fit in a teacup.Pygmy shrew: One of the smallest mammals, it must eat nearly constantly, almost its own weight in food each day.

Animals that could fit in a teacup.Bee: Bees see ultraviolet light and can recognize human faces, in a brain the size of a sesame seed.
Animals that could fit in a teacup.Ant: An ant can carry about 50 times its own weight, and ant colonies can span continents.
Animals that could fit in a teacup.Butterfly: Butterflies taste with their feet, and they can fit on a fingertip.

Animals that could fit in a teacup.Cricket: You can estimate the temperature by counting chirps, a rule known as Dolbear's law.
Animals that could fit in a teacup.Firefly: Fireflies make light with almost no heat, and the glow is cold light that is among the most efficient known.
Animals that could fit in a teacup.Cat: A trap: even a small adult cat is far too big for a teacup, whatever the internet claims.
Animals that could fit in a teacup.Rabbit: A trap: even the tiniest breed is too big, and rabbits don't curl up to fit a cup.
Animals that could fit in a teacup.Penguin: Even the smallest penguin, the little penguin, stands about 30 centimeters tall.
Animals that could fit in a teacup.Owl: Even a tiny elf owl, about 13 centimeters tall, is too big for a teacup, though not by much.
Animals that could fit in a teacup.Squirrel: Too big: even a small red squirrel is about 20 centimeters long, not counting its tail.
Animals that could fit in a teacup.Parrot: Even the smallest parrots are too big; African grey parrots can learn hundreds of words and are about 33 centimeters long.
Animals that could fit in a teacup.Ferret: A ferret is over 40 centimeters of long, flexible body, so it won't fit in a cup, though it can squeeze through tight tunnels.

Animals that could fit in a teacup.Fox: The smallest fox, the fennec, weighs around 1.5 kilograms, far too big for a teacup.
Animals that could fit in a teacup.Pigeon: Pigeons can find their way home from hundreds of kilometers away, and they're about 30 centimeters long.
Animals that could fit in a teacup.Iguana: A green iguana can grow over 1.5 meters from nose to tail, far too long for a teacup, and it can drop its tail to escape.

National capitals in Africa.Tunis: Tunisia's capital lies close to the ruins of ancient Carthage.

Things you'd find in a hot desert.Cactus: Almost all cacti are native to the Americas, so a cactus in a Sahara scene is a misplaced prop; a saguaro can take 50 to 75 years to grow its first arm.
Things you'd find in a hot desert.Oasis: An oasis forms where underground water reaches the surface; Egypt's Siwa has supported farming and towns for thousands of years.
Things you'd find in a hot desert.Sand dune: Even in the Sahara, sand covers only about a fifth of the surface; most desert is bare rock and gravel.
Things you'd find in a hot desert.Camel: A thirsty dromedary can gulp well over 100 liters of water in just minutes, then go days without another drink.
Things you'd find in a hot desert.Mirage: A mirage is real light bent by hot air near the ground, so cameras can photograph it; it's not a hallucination.
Things you'd find in a hot desert.Scorpion: Scorpions glow blue-green under ultraviolet light, which is how desert researchers find them at night.
Things you'd find in a hot desert.Tumbleweed: The tumbleweed is Russian thistle, an invader that reached South Dakota in the 1870s in contaminated flaxseed.
Things you'd find in a hot desert.Wadi: A wadi is a dry riverbed that can flood suddenly from rain falling miles away, which has caught many travellers off guard.
Things you'd find in a hot desert.Rattlesnake: A rattlesnake adds a rattle segment each time it sheds, but segments break off, so the rattle can't tell its age.
Things you'd find in a hot desert.Sandstorm: Saharan dust storms carry enough dust across the Atlantic to fertilize the Amazon rainforest.
Things you'd find in a hot desert.Fennec fox: The fennec fox, the smallest canid, uses its huge ears to shed heat and hear prey moving beneath the sand.
Things you'd find in a hot desert.Roadrunner: The greater roadrunner can sprint around 20 miles per hour and kills rattlesnakes by pecking and pinning them.
Things you'd find in a hot desert.Iceberg: Icebergs belong to polar seas, the opposite of a hot desert, and about nine-tenths of each one is underwater.
Things you'd find in a hot desert.Glacier: Glaciers are rivers of slowly flowing ice, and need cold and snow, which hot deserts lack.
Things you'd find in a hot desert.Penguin: Most penguins live in cool southern waters; even the Galápagos penguin, which lives at the equator, relies on cold currents, not desert.
Things you'd find in a hot desert.Polar bear: Polar bears hunt on Arctic sea ice, and their skin is black beneath translucent fur.
Things you'd find in a hot desert.Coral reef: Coral reefs are warm-water marine ecosystems, not desert, and they're built by tiny animals called polyps.
Things you'd find in a hot desert.Kelp: Kelp is a giant brown seaweed of cool coastal waters, and some species can grow half a meter a day.
Things you'd find in a hot desert.Walrus: Walruses live in the Arctic, hauling out on ice, and use their tusks to climb on it.
Things you'd find in a hot desert.Igloo: The igloo is an Inuit snow house, and the snow's trapped air insulates well enough to stay above freezing inside.
Things you'd find in a hot desert.Fjord: Fjords are deep sea inlets carved by glaciers, found in cold places like Norway and New Zealand.
Things you'd find in a hot desert.Mangrove: Mangroves grow in salty tropical coastal swamps, with roots that stand in tidal water, not in dry desert.
Things you'd find in a hot desert.Narwhal: A narwhal's 'tusk' is actually a long tooth, and these Arctic whales belong to icy waters.
Things you'd find in a hot desert.Sea otter: Sea otters have the densest fur of any animal, up to about a million hairs per square inch, and live in cool northern seas.

Mixtures (not pure substances).Air: Air is about 78 percent nitrogen and 21 percent oxygen, plus argon and traces. It's a mixture, not a compound.
Mixtures (not pure substances).Salad: A salad is a mechanical mixture where you can see and pick out each part, in contrast to a solution where parts are blended.
Mixtures (not pure substances).Seawater: Seawater is about 3.5 percent dissolved salts, mostly sodium chloride. Evaporating it leaves the salts behind, a basic separation method.
Mixtures (not pure substances).Milk: Milk is water holding tiny fat droplets and proteins suspended in it. Homogenizing breaks the fat into particles so cream doesn't rise.
Mixtures (not pure substances).Soil: Soil mixes minerals, organic matter, water, air and living organisms. A single teaspoon can hold billions of microbes.
Mixtures (not pure substances).Granite: Granite is a mixture of crystals of quartz, feldspar and mica, and you can see them as flecks on a countertop.
Mixtures (not pure substances).Concrete: Concrete mixes cement, sand, gravel and water. Cement chemistry hardens it, and the Romans' recipe has lasted two thousand years.
Mixtures (not pure substances).Blood: Blood is cells floating in plasma, a mixture that can be spun in a centrifuge to separate red cells from the liquid.
Mixtures (not pure substances).Trail mix: A classic example of a heterogeneous mixture, and you can separate each part by hand, with no chemistry involved.
Mixtures (not pure substances).Soda: Soda is sugar, flavorings and dissolved carbon dioxide in water. Opening the can drops the pressure, so the gas escapes as bubbles.
Mixtures (not pure substances).Bronze: Bronze is an alloy, a solid mixture of mostly copper and tin. It was so important that it named an entire era of history.
Mixtures (not pure substances).Distilled water: Distilled water is just H2O, nothing else. Being pure, it contains no minerals, so it tastes flat.
Mixtures (not pure substances).Oxygen: Oxygen as a gas of O2 is a pure element. Pure oxygen is far more flammable than the air we breathe.
Mixtures (not pure substances).Gold: Pure gold is an element. 24-karat means essentially pure, while 18-karat gold is an alloy and therefore a mixture.
Mixtures (not pure substances).Sodium chloride: Table salt is a compound with a fixed 1:1 ratio of sodium to chloride. That fixed ratio is what separates compounds from mixtures.
Mixtures (not pure substances).Sugar: Sucrose, pure table sugar, is a compound with a fixed formula. Sugar solution would be a mixture, but the crystals alone aren't.
Mixtures (not pure substances).Diamond: Diamond is pure carbon, which makes it a pure substance. It's the same element as the graphite in a pencil, arranged differently.
Mixtures (not pure substances).Carbon dioxide: CO2 is a compound with a fixed ratio of one carbon to two oxygen atoms, making it a pure substance rather than a mixture.
Mixtures (not pure substances).Iron: Iron is an element, a pure substance. Steel, in contrast, is iron mixed with a little carbon, which makes it a mixture.
Mixtures (not pure substances).Helium: Helium is a single element and a pure substance. It's the second most abundant element in the universe, after hydrogen.
Mixtures (not pure substances).Baking soda: Sodium bicarbonate is a chemical compound with a fixed formula, so it's a pure substance even though it sits in your kitchen.
Mixtures (not pure substances).Aluminum: Aluminum is an element, a pure substance. Once more precious than gold, it became cheap only after electrolysis in the 1880s.
Mixtures (not pure substances).Copper: Copper is an element, a pure substance. Mixed with zinc it becomes brass, and with tin it becomes bronze, which are mixtures.
Mixtures (not pure substances).Neon: Neon is a pure element, a noble gas that glows red-orange in a tube. Most neon signs in other colors use other gases or coatings.

Things a plant needs to grow.Sunlight: Plants capture it with chlorophyll, which reflects green light. That's why leaves look green: the pigment absorbs the other colors.
Things a plant needs to grow.Water: A plant uses very little of the water it takes up for growth. Nearly all of it evaporates through leaves in a process called transpiration.
Things a plant needs to grow.Carbon dioxide: Plants build their own bodies mostly from carbon taken from the air. A tree's wood is largely carbon dioxide made solid.
Things a plant needs to grow.Nitrogen: Nitrogen is the N in fertilizer's N-P-K label, vital for green growth. Beans and peas get it with help from bacteria on their roots.
Things a plant needs to grow.Phosphorus: The P in fertilizer's N-P-K, phosphorus fuels roots, flowers and energy transfer in cells. Mined phosphate rock is a limited resource.
Things a plant needs to grow.Potassium: The K in N-P-K, potassium regulates the tiny pores on leaves that open and close for gas exchange.
Things a plant needs to grow.Oxygen: Plants make oxygen but also need it, as their roots breathe it and the plant uses it at night. Waterlogged soil can drown roots.
Things a plant needs to grow.Magnesium: Magnesium sits at the center of every chlorophyll molecule. Without it, leaves turn yellow between the veins.
Things a plant needs to grow.Iron: Plants need iron in small amounts to make chlorophyll. A shortage turns new leaves pale yellow, a problem called chlorosis.
Things a plant needs to grow.Calcium: Calcium builds cell walls, and shortages cause problems like blossom end rot in tomatoes, which makes the bottom of the fruit turn dark.
Things a plant needs to grow.Sulfur: Sulfur is part of some amino acids and gives onions, garlic and mustard their sharp bite.
Things a plant needs to grow.Gold: Gold plays no known role in plant growth. A few plants can absorb tiny amounts from soil, a trick researchers have explored for prospecting.
Things a plant needs to grow.Lead: Lead is toxic to plants and people, and no plant needs it. Plants can take it up from contaminated soil, which is a food safety worry.
Things a plant needs to grow.Helium: Helium is an inert gas that plants don't use. It's so light that it escapes Earth's atmosphere into space.
Things a plant needs to grow.Neon: Neon is a noble gas that doesn't react with anything, so plants can't use it and it plays no role in their biology.
Things a plant needs to grow.Uranium: Uranium isn't a plant nutrient, and it's radioactive. Some plants, though, can absorb it, a trick used to clean contaminated soil.
Things a plant needs to grow.Plutonium: Plutonium is a radioactive metal made in reactors, with no role in biology. Plants have no use for it and it is toxic.
Things a plant needs to grow.Mercury: Mercury is toxic and not a nutrient. It stunts plants and builds up in food chains, especially in fish.
Things a plant needs to grow.Music: Despite the popular belief, there's no solid proof that music boosts plant growth. Lab results are mixed, and plants don't need it.
Things a plant needs to grow.Arsenic: Arsenic is poisonous, and rice plants can take it up from soil and water, which is why rice is checked for it.
Things a plant needs to grow.Plastic: Plastic isn't a nutrient, and it gets into soil as microplastic. It can be harmful to the soil life that plants rely on.
Things a plant needs to grow.Platinum: Platinum is a precious metal that plants don't need. It's rarer than gold and used in catalytic converters.
Things a plant needs to grow.Silver: Silver is not a nutrient and is even toxic to many microbes, which is why it's put on bandages. Plants don't need it.
Things a plant needs to grow.Krypton: Krypton is a noble gas that doesn't react, so no plant can use it. Its name comes from the Greek for hidden.

Superheroes who wear a cape.Batman: Bruce Wayne's cape is designed to look like bat wings, and in the comics it can glide or be stiffened.
Superheroes who wear a cape.Thor: The Marvel version's red cape and winged helm come from the Norse god, but his real power is in his hammer Mjolnir.
Superheroes who wear a cape.Doctor Strange: The Cloak of Levitation is a sentient relic that picks its wearer and flies him around, and in the films it has a mind of its own.
Superheroes who wear a cape.Supergirl: Superman's cousin Kara Zor-El is from Krypton, and she wears the family's famous red cape.
Superheroes who wear a cape.Vision: The synthezoid Avenger has worn a cape in both the comics and the films, a green-and-gold cloak that suits his regal presence.
Superheroes who wear a cape.Shazam: Billy Batson says the wizard's name and becomes a red-suited hero with a golden lightning bolt and a white cape.
Superheroes who wear a cape.Robin: Dick Grayson, the first Robin, appeared in 1940, and his yellow cape added color to Batman's dark world.
Superheroes who wear a cape.Batgirl: Barbara Gordon's cowled cape appeared in 1967, and she became Oracle after being shot by the Joker in The Killing Joke.
Superheroes who wear a cape.Underdog: The cartoon dog hero from 1964 spoke in rhymes and wore a red cape, with the catchphrase 'There's no need to fear'.
Superheroes who wear a cape.Mighty Mouse: The caped cartoon mouse was created in 1942 as a parody of Superman, originally named Super Mouse.
Superheroes who wear a cape.Captain Underpants: Dav Pilkey's hero is a principal hypnotized by two fourth-graders. He flies in a red cape and white briefs.
Superheroes who wear a cape.Spider-Man: A cape would tangle in his webs while swinging through the city, so his costume is just a suit, and the mask keeps his identity secret.
Superheroes who wear a cape.Iron Man: Tony Stark's armor is a powered suit with no flowing cloth to snag in the repulsors, and he's a flier without a cape.
Superheroes who wear a cape.Hulk: The Hulk wears only stretchy purple pants, a running gag since the fabric survives his transformations, and he never wears a cape.
Superheroes who wear a cape.Wolverine: The mutant's classic yellow-and-blue suit has a cowl and claws, and no cape. He is meant to be a brawler, not a flier.
Superheroes who wear a cape.The Flash: The Scarlet Speedster's skintight suit has no cape. A cape would flap and drag at speeds near the speed of light.
Superheroes who wear a cape.Captain America: Cap has a shield and star on his chest. A cape would only get in the way in close-quarters fighting.
Superheroes who wear a cape.Black Widow: Natasha Romanoff is a spy, and her catsuit is built for stealth and agility, which is a poor fit for a cape.
Superheroes who wear a cape.Aquaman: The king of Atlantis wears orange and green, and a cape would just drift behind him in the water.
Superheroes who wear a cape.Hawkeye: Clint Barton relies on a bow and trick arrows, and has no cape. His best asset is his skill, not any superpowers.
Superheroes who wear a cape.Deadpool: The red-and-black suit hides his scars. He carries swords and guns, but no cape, a note also from the comics.
Superheroes who wear a cape.Mr. Incredible: Edna Mode famously declares 'No capes!' after seeing heroes die when theirs got caught, so his suit stays cape-free.
Superheroes who wear a cape.Frozone: Lucius Best also follows Edna Mode's rule 'No capes!', and he is the only one of the Incredibles heroes whose suit stays sleek.

James Bond theme songs.Goldfinger: Shirley Bassey's 1964 showstopper set the brassy template for Bond themes, and she went on to sing two more.
James Bond theme songs.Skyfall: Adele's 2012 theme won the Oscar for Best Original Song, the first Bond theme ever to take that prize.
James Bond theme songs.Live and Let Die: Paul McCartney and Wings recorded it in 1973, produced by George Martin; it earned an Oscar nomination and a famous orchestral middle section.
James Bond theme songs.Diamonds Are Forever: Shirley Bassey's second Bond theme, 1971, by composer John Barry. Kanye West later sampled it for Diamonds from Sierra Leone.
James Bond theme songs.A View to a Kill: Duran Duran's 1985 theme is the only Bond song to reach number one on the US Billboard Hot 100.
James Bond theme songs.GoldenEye: Tina Turner sang this 1995 theme, written for her by Bono and The Edge of U2.
James Bond theme songs.No Time to Die: Billie Eilish wrote it with her brother Finneas as a teenager; it won the Oscar for Best Original Song.
James Bond theme songs.Thunderball: Tom Jones belted this 1965 theme so hard that, as the story goes, he fainted after holding the last note.
James Bond theme songs.Licence to Kill: Gladys Knight sang this 1989 theme. The film was nearly titled Licence Revoked before the name was changed.
James Bond theme songs.Die Another Day: Madonna sang this 2002 theme and also popped up in the film itself as a fencing instructor.
James Bond theme songs.You Know My Name: Chris Cornell's 2006 Casino Royale theme is a trap: it is a real Bond song, yet its title isn't the film's name.
James Bond theme songs.Moonraker: Shirley Bassey's third and last Bond theme, from the 1979 space-set film, scored by John Barry.
James Bond theme songs.The Living Daylights: Norwegian band a-ha sang this 1987 theme, and reportedly clashed with composer John Barry over the final sound.
James Bond theme songs.Eye of the Tiger: Survivor wrote it for Rocky III after Sylvester Stallone asked them for a theme, so it belongs to boxing, not Bond.
James Bond theme songs.My Heart Will Go On: Celine Dion's 1997 Titanic ballad won an Oscar and was composed by James Horner, not by any Bond team.
James Bond theme songs.Ghostbusters: Ray Parker Jr.'s 1984 hit was so close to Huey Lewis's I Want a New Drug that Lewis sued; it still never touched Bond.
James Bond theme songs.Footloose: Kenny Loggins sang this 1984 title song for a film about a town that banned dancing; no spies involved.
James Bond theme songs.Take My Breath Away: Berlin's 1986 Top Gun ballad won the Oscar for Best Original Song, but it's a love song for pilots, not a Bond theme.
James Bond theme songs.Danger Zone: Another Kenny Loggins anthem, this one from Top Gun; Giorgio Moroder co-wrote it, but it has no 007 link.
James Bond theme songs.Stayin' Alive: The Bee Gees' beat of roughly 103 per minute is the one health workers use to practise CPR; Bond never used it.
James Bond theme songs.Purple Rain: Prince's 1984 title track was recorded live at First Avenue in Minneapolis, far from any Bond soundtrack.
James Bond theme songs.What a Feeling: Irene Cara's Flashdance theme won an Oscar, which makes it award-winning like Skyfall but not a Bond song.
James Bond theme songs.Pink Panther Theme: Henry Mancini's sneaky tune suits a spy mood, which makes it a trap, but it belongs to a bumbling cartoon-style inspector.
James Bond theme songs.Lose Yourself: Eminem's 8 Mile song was the first rap track to win the Oscar for Best Original Song.

Parts of a pop song.Verse: From Latin for 'a turn', the verse is where the song's story unfolds, usually over the same melody each time.
Parts of a pop song.Chorus: From the Greek for 'dance', it's the bit everyone can sing along to, the part of a song that repeats.
Parts of a pop song.Bridge: A contrasting section, often after the second chorus, that gives a song a new twist before the finale.
Parts of a pop song.Intro: Hooks in the first seconds matter: with streaming, intros have become much shorter than in the 1980s.
Parts of a pop song.Outro: The closing section of a song, often a fade or a final repeat, that lets the music wind down.
Parts of a pop song.Hook: The catchy bit that gets stuck in your head, and songwriters use it like fishing.
Parts of a pop song.Refrain: A line or phrase repeated at the end of each verse; unlike a chorus, a refrain is often just a short line.
Parts of a pop song.Pre-chorus: A short build between verse and chorus, which raises tension so the chorus lands harder.
Parts of a pop song.Coda: Italian for 'tail', it's an extended ending that wraps up a song or movement.
Parts of a pop song.Middle eight: Typically eight bars long, it offers a break and a change of mood, famously used by The Beatles.
Parts of a pop song.Interlude: A short instrumental or quiet passage that connects two sections, giving listeners a breather.
Parts of a pop song.Chapter: Latin capitulum means 'little head', and novels split into chapters, which is a book idea.
Parts of a pop song.Paragraph: Greek for 'written beside', it began as a margin mark showing a break in text, not a song section.
Parts of a pop song.Footnote: A note at the bottom of a page, born from medieval marginal notes, belongs to books, not songs.
Parts of a pop song.Prologue: Greek for 'before word', Shakespeare opened Romeo and Juliet with one, and it's a story piece.
Parts of a pop song.Act: Plays divide into acts, Shakespeare's usually five, but songs don't.
Parts of a pop song.Scene: Greek skene was the hut behind the stage, and scenes belong to plays and films.
Parts of a pop song.Headline: Headlines are usually written by editors, not the reporters, and belong to news, not song.
Parts of a pop song.Preface: A preface is written by the author; a foreword by someone else, and neither fits a song.
Parts of a pop song.Index: Latin for 'pointer', which is why it names your index finger, and books have them at the back.
Parts of a pop song.Appendix: Also a small organ in your body, though here it's the extra section at a book's end.
Parts of a pop song.Sonnet: A 14-line poem; Shakespeare wrote 154 of them, but it's poetry, not a song section.
Parts of a pop song.Caption: Text under a picture, a captioning job, not a part of a pop song.
Parts of a pop song.Epilogue: A closing section after the story; the Harry Potter series ends with one set 19 years later.

NHL team nicknames.Maple Leafs: Toronto last won the Stanley Cup in 1967; the team's name honors Canada's maple leaf emblem worn by soldiers in WWI.
NHL team nicknames.Bruins: Boston was the first US team in the NHL, joining in 1924, and is one of the Original Six.
NHL team nicknames.Canadiens: Montreal has won the Stanley Cup 24 times, the most of any franchise, and its nickname is 'Habs'.
NHL team nicknames.Blackhawks: Chicago's name honors the Black Hawk Division of WWI, named for Sauk leader Black Hawk.
NHL team nicknames.Red Wings: Detroit's winged-wheel logo reflects the city's car-making identity, and the team is known as 'Hockeytown'.
NHL team nicknames.Penguins: Pittsburgh won back-to-back Cups in 2016 and 2017, with Sidney Crosby and Evgeni Malkin.
NHL team nicknames.Oilers: Edmonton, with Wayne Gretzky, won five Cups between 1984 and 1990, and the name nods to Alberta's oil industry.
NHL team nicknames.Flyers: Philadelphia's 'Broad Street Bullies' won the Stanley Cup in 1974 and 1975, and the team's mascot is Gritty.
NHL team nicknames.Canucks: Vancouver's name is slang for Canadians, and the team has reached the Stanley Cup final three times without winning.
NHL team nicknames.Lightning: Tampa Bay's name honors Florida's lightning-strike frequency; they won back-to-back Cups in 2020 and 2021.
NHL team nicknames.Capitals: Washington's Alex Ovechkin finally won the Cup in 2018, after 13 seasons.
NHL team nicknames.Avalanche: The Quebec Nordiques moved to Denver in 1995 and became the Avalanche, winning the Cup that same year.
NHL team nicknames.Sabres: Buffalo's name was picked in a fan contest, and the team has never won the Cup.
NHL team nicknames.Lakers: An NBA team, whose name came from Minnesota's lakes, not an NHL team.
NHL team nicknames.Yankees: New York's baseball team, with 27 World Series titles, so not a hockey club.
NHL team nicknames.Packers: An NFL team from Green Bay, named after a meatpacking company, not a hockey club.
NHL team nicknames.Bulls: An NBA team from Chicago, whose NHL equivalent is the Blackhawks.
NHL team nicknames.Celtics: An NBA team from Boston, where the NHL side is the Bruins.
NHL team nicknames.Cubs: A Chicago baseball team that ended a 108-year title drought in 2016; Chicago's hockey side is the Blackhawks.
NHL team nicknames.Raptors: Toronto's NBA team, which won the 2019 title, and not a hockey side like the Maple Leafs.
NHL team nicknames.Blue Jays: Toronto's baseball team, which won back-to-back World Series in 1992 and 1993, not an NHL club.
NHL team nicknames.Steelers: Pittsburgh's NFL team, not the city's hockey team, the Penguins.
NHL team nicknames.Dodgers: A baseball team that moved from Brooklyn to Los Angeles in 1958, so not an NHL team.
NHL team nicknames.Knicks: A New York NBA team, short for Knickerbockers, not hockey; New York's NHL sides are the Rangers and Islanders.

Transformed by the Greek gods.Arachne: A weaver who challenged Athena and lost, and became the first spider; arachnids are named for her.
Transformed by the Greek gods.Narcissus: He pined away over his own reflection and became the flower; 'narcissism' comes from the tale.
Transformed by the Greek gods.Daphne: She became a laurel tree to escape Apollo's pursuit, and the laurel wreath stayed his emblem forever.
Transformed by the Greek gods.Io: Zeus turned her into a cow to hide her from Hera, who then sent a gadfly to torment her across the world.
Transformed by the Greek gods.Callisto: A nymph in Artemis's company, she was changed into a bear; Zeus placed her in the sky as Ursa Major.
Transformed by the Greek gods.Actaeon: A hunter who glimpsed Artemis bathing, was turned into a stag and was torn apart by his own hounds.
Transformed by the Greek gods.Niobe: After boasting about her many children over Leto's two, she was left childless and turned to weeping stone.
Transformed by the Greek gods.Lycaon: A king of Arcadia who served Zeus human flesh at a feast, and was turned into a wolf; 'lycanthropy' comes from his name.
Transformed by the Greek gods.Hyacinthus: Apollo's beloved, accidentally killed by a discus, from whose blood the hyacinth flower rose.
Transformed by the Greek gods.Syrinx: A nymph fleeing Pan who became reeds, from which Pan made the panpipes, also called a syrinx.
Transformed by the Greek gods.Medusa: In Ovid's telling, Athena turned this beautiful woman into a snake-haired Gorgon after Poseidon assaulted her in Athena's temple.
Transformed by the Greek gods.Achilles: A trap: he was a mortal warrior who was never transformed; he died by an arrow in the heel.
Transformed by the Greek gods.Perseus: A trap: a hero, but he never changed shape; he turned others to stone with Medusa's head.
Transformed by the Greek gods.Odysseus: Circe turned his men into pigs, but he escaped, protected by the herb moly, and was not transformed.
Transformed by the Greek gods.Penelope: A trap: Odysseus's wife waited twenty years and stayed a human woman, with no transformation in her story.
Transformed by the Greek gods.Jason: A trap: the Argonauts' leader kept his human form, and met his end when a rotting beam of the Argo fell on him.
Transformed by the Greek gods.Theseus: A trap: the Athenian hero killed the Minotaur and stayed a man, ending as a king of Athens.
Transformed by the Greek gods.Helen: A trap: the beauty whose abduction sparked the Trojan War stayed fully human in Greek stories.
Transformed by the Greek gods.Paris: A trap: the Trojan prince who judged the golden apple contest was never changed into anything.
Transformed by the Greek gods.Hector: A trap: Troy's champion was killed by Achilles and dragged behind his chariot, but never transformed.
Transformed by the Greek gods.Oedipus: A trap: he blinded himself in horror, a human tragedy rather than a transformation by the gods.
Transformed by the Greek gods.Icarus: His fate was falling into the sea, not a transformation, so he doesn't belong; the Icarian Sea is named for him.
Transformed by the Greek gods.Antigone: A trap: she defied King Creon to bury her brother and died human, a victim of law, not a transformation.
Transformed by the Greek gods.Agamemnon: A trap: the king of Mycenae was killed in his bath by his wife, and no god ever changed his form.

Siege engines.Trebuchet: Edward I's giant Warwolf trebuchet helped take Stirling Castle in 1304, and its counterweight design out-threw older catapults.
Siege engines.Catapult: Engineers of Dionysius of Syracuse are credited with inventing the catapult around 399 BC.
Siege engines.Battering ram: Rams were roofed with wet hides to protect their crews from fire and arrows.
Siege engines.Ballista: A giant crossbow whose power came from twisted sinew or hair rope, able to pierce shields and armor.
Siege engines.Mangonel: Powered by twisted rope, it flung rocks in a high arc, and it's often confused with the trebuchet.
Siege engines.Siege tower: Wooden towers covered in wet hides rolled up to the walls, as Alexander the Great used at Tyre in 332 BC.
Siege engines.Onager: Named for the wild ass for its kick, this Roman stone-thrower recoiled violently when fired.
Siege engines.Scorpio: Roman bolt shooter whose name means 'scorpion', a small, accurate piece of artillery.
Siege engines.Siege ladder: Simple but deadly; attackers climbed under fire while defenders pushed ladders away with forked poles.
Siege engines.Tank: Invented in 1916, it was called a 'tank' as cover story to disguise it as a water tank.
Siege engines.Musket: A firearm is a personal weapon, and a musket was carried by one soldier rather than a siege machine.
Siege engines.Halberd: An axe-and-spike on a pole, carried by one soldier, not a machine to batter walls.
Siege engines.Longbow: The longbow's arrows won Agincourt in 1415, but it was a hand weapon, not an engine.
Siege engines.Lance: A knight's weapon for charging on horseback, not a machine for assaulting walls.
Siege engines.Mace: A handheld club, whose descendant is the ceremonial mace in Parliament.
Siege engines.Pike: Long spear carried by one soldier; Swiss pike squares dominated battlefields.
Siege engines.Flail: A threshing tool turned weapon, held by a single fighter.
Siege engines.Morning star: A spiked club carried in hand, not a siege machine.
Siege engines.Chariot: Chariots were battlefield vehicles that were useless against walls.
Siege engines.Bulldozer: Invented in the 1920s, so too late for medieval castles.
Siege engines.Drawbridge: A defender's feature that could be raised to block attackers.
Siege engines.Portcullis: The Parliament emblem is a portcullis, a grille defenders dropped; it's defense, not attack.
Siege engines.Moat: It's a defensive ditch that stopped siege towers and rams, and also tunnelers.
Siege engines.Zeppelin: Zeppelins were airships from 1900 and bombers in World War I, not medieval engines.

Pans you use on the stovetop.Saucepan: A saucepan has tall straight sides and a long handle, ideal for sauces, boiling eggs, or heating milk.
Pans you use on the stovetop.Frying pan: Frying pans use a wide base for good contact, and a non-stick coating means food slides off without sticking.
Pans you use on the stovetop.Wok: A wok's curved bowl gives hot and cooler zones, and cooks have used one in China for around two thousand years.
Pans you use on the stovetop.Stockpot: A stockpot is tall and narrow so liquid evaporates slowly while stock simmers for hours.
Pans you use on the stovetop.Skillet: Skillet is a more American word for a frying pan, and cast iron versions can last for generations.
Pans you use on the stovetop.Griddle: A griddle is a flat plate with no sides, and its name comes from an old word for a gridiron.
Pans you use on the stovetop.Saute pan: Sauté means jump in French, and the pan has straight sides to hold ingredients as they are tossed.
Pans you use on the stovetop.Double boiler: A double boiler heats the top bowl with steam, which gently melts chocolate without scorching it.
Pans you use on the stovetop.Crepe pan: A crepe pan is wide and nearly flat, with a very low rim so you can slide a spatula under the thin batter.
Pans you use on the stovetop.Grill pan: A grill pan has ridges that leave sear marks and let fat drain below the food.
Pans you use on the stovetop.Baking sheet: A baking sheet is a flat metal tray made for the oven, and warping happens when it heats unevenly.
Pans you use on the stovetop.Muffin tin: A muffin tin shapes batter into cups, and it is meant for the oven.
Pans you use on the stovetop.Colander: A colander is a bowl with holes that drains pasta water, and it is never used for heating.
Pans you use on the stovetop.Mixing bowl: A mixing bowl holds ingredients and is not made to go on a flame, particularly if it is glass or ceramic.
Pans you use on the stovetop.Cutting board: A cutting board is for chopping, and wood boards can be gentler on knives than plastic.
Pans you use on the stovetop.Pie dish: A pie dish is glass, ceramic or metal and is meant for the oven, where it cooks the crust.
Pans you use on the stovetop.Loaf tin: A loaf tin shapes bread and cake in the oven and is not meant for a burner.
Pans you use on the stovetop.Ramekin: A ramekin is a little ceramic cup for oven dishes such as crème brûlée and soufflé.
Pans you use on the stovetop.Salad bowl: A salad bowl is for serving cold food, so heat would crack wooden or ceramic ones.
Pans you use on the stovetop.Cake tin: A cake tin goes in the oven and is not designed for direct stovetop heat.
Pans you use on the stovetop.Springform pan: A springform pan has a clasp that releases the side, so delicate cheesecakes lift out without flipping.
Pans you use on the stovetop.Bundt pan: A Bundt pan gives cakes their ring shape and was popularized by a Minnesota company in 1950.
Pans you use on the stovetop.Cookie sheet: A cookie sheet is a flat tray with lips or none, and goes in the oven only.
Pans you use on the stovetop.Pizza stone: A pizza stone sits in a hot oven and absorbs moisture to crisp the crust, but a flame can crack it.

Body parts you have exactly one of.Heart: You have one heart, which beats about 100,000 times a day, and it sits slightly left of center.
Body parts you have exactly one of.Liver: The liver is your largest internal organ, weighing about 1.5 kilograms, and you only have one.
Body parts you have exactly one of.Nose: You have just one nose, though it has two nostrils, which are a trap here since they come as a pair.
Body parts you have exactly one of.Navel: The navel is the scar of the umbilical cord, and everyone has just one, though shapes differ.
Body parts you have exactly one of.Spleen: You have one spleen on the left side, which filters blood and helps fight infection.
Body parts you have exactly one of.Stomach: The stomach is a single J-shaped organ that holds about a liter and a half when full.
Body parts you have exactly one of.Tongue: The tongue is one muscle bundle, even though it appears to have two halves, split down the middle.
Body parts you have exactly one of.Bladder: There's one bladder, which stores urine and can stretch to hold around half a liter.
Body parts you have exactly one of.Appendix: The appendix is a single pouch off the large intestine, and many people have it removed.
Body parts you have exactly one of.Pancreas: The pancreas is a single flat gland tucked behind the stomach.
Body parts you have exactly one of.Chin: You have a single chin, even though some people have a cleft one that looks like two.
Body parts you have exactly one of.Uvula: The uvula is the single dangling flap at the back of the throat, and the word means little grape.
Body parts you have exactly one of.Kidney: You have two kidneys, though one is enough to live, so it isn't a single organ.
Body parts you have exactly one of.Lung: Humans have two lungs, and the left one is smaller to make room for the heart.
Body parts you have exactly one of.Eye: You have two eyes, which help perceive depth.
Body parts you have exactly one of.Ear: You have two ears, and having two helps you tell which way a sound is coming from.
Body parts you have exactly one of.Elbow: Everyone has two elbows, and you can't lick yours: that famous myth is a decent party trick for a joint almost nobody can reach.
Body parts you have exactly one of.Thumb: You have two thumbs, and each has just two bones, while every other finger has three, which is part of why the thumb is so strong.
Body parts you have exactly one of.Eyebrow: Eyebrows come in pairs, and they help keep sweat and rain out of your eyes.
Body parts you have exactly one of.Nostril: Nostrils come in pairs, and they alternate dominance in airflow every few hours.
Body parts you have exactly one of.Collarbone: You have two collarbones, and the clavicle is among the most commonly broken bones.
Body parts you have exactly one of.Knee: You have two knees, the largest joints in the body.
Body parts you have exactly one of.Tonsil: You have two tonsils, which sit on either side of the throat.
Body parts you have exactly one of.Cheek: You have two cheeks, so this is a pair, not a single part.

Things that bounce.Rubber ball: Rubber's bounce comes from long, tangled molecules that stretch and snap back, a property called elasticity.
Things that bounce.Basketball: A regulation basketball should bounce back to about half to two thirds of the height it was dropped from, and it is tested that way.
Things that bounce.Tennis ball: Tennis balls are pressurized, and when they go flat they lose bounce; sealed cans keep the pressure in.
Things that bounce.Pogo stick: The pogo stick's spring was patented in Germany in 1920 by Max Pohlig and Ernst Gottschall, and it is said to be named after Pohlig's nickname.
Things that bounce.Kangaroo: Kangaroos bounce by storing energy in their tendons, which spring like rubber bands, so hopping fast costs them little extra energy.
Things that bounce.Bouncy ball: The Super Ball was invented in 1964 by chemist Norman Stingley and could bounce about 90 percent of its drop height.
Things that bounce.Ping-pong ball: A table tennis ball weighs just 2.7 grams and bounces off the table at close to 90 percent of the height it fell from.
Things that bounce.Soccer ball: Modern soccer balls are made of stitched or glued panels around a bladder, and inflated balls keep their shape with air.
Things that bounce.Volleyball: A volleyball is light, about 260 to 280 grams, and its inflation level is carefully set so it bounces predictably.
Things that bounce.Space hopper: The space hopper, a ride-on inflatable ball with ears, was a craze in 1970s Britain, based on an Italian design.
Things that bounce.Tigger: Tigger, A. A. Milne's bouncy tiger from Winnie-the-Pooh, famously says that bouncing is what Tiggers do best.
Things that bounce.Egg: An egg's shell is strong in compression but cracks easily when dropped; in the right conditions you can make a pickled egg bounce, but a raw one splatters.
Things that bounce.Watermelon: A watermelon is about 92 percent water and bursts when dropped; it is no bouncer, though a ripe one can bounce a short distance.
Things that bounce.Wine glass: A wine glass is thin, brittle glass that shatters instead of bouncing, though a strong enough note can actually break it.
Things that bounce.Pancake: A pancake is a soft, flat, floppy thing that just lands with a plop, though an American-style one is slightly springy.
Things that bounce.Brick: A brick is dense and hard, so it lands with a thud and doesn't rebound, though it often cracks.
Things that bounce.Cake: Cake is soft, crumbly, and full of air pockets, so it squashes when dropped instead of rebounding.
Things that bounce.Banana: A banana is soft, so it bruises and squishes on impact rather than bouncing, and the peel adds its own slippery risk.
Things that bounce.Tomato: A ripe tomato is soft and full of juice, so it splatters on landing, which is why it was the classic stage-throwing item.
Things that bounce.Dinner plate: A ceramic dinner plate is brittle, so a drop onto a hard floor usually ends in many broken pieces, not a bounce.
Things that bounce.Light bulb: A light bulb is thin glass around a vacuum or gas, so it pops loudly and shatters when it hits the floor.
Things that bounce.Sandbag: A sandbag is built to soak up impact and sit still; the sand shifts and absorbs energy so it doesn't rebound.
Things that bounce.Anvil: An anvil is dense hard steel that doesn't compress, so it lands with a thud and a dent in the floor rather than rebounding.
Things that bounce.Sock: A sock is soft cloth that drops lifelessly, though a balled-up pair of socks can bounce slightly.

Things Santa needs on Christmas Eve.Sleigh: Santa's sleigh first flew in the 1823 poem A Visit from St. Nicholas, which also gave the reindeer their names.
Things Santa needs on Christmas Eve.Reindeer: Reindeer are the only deer in which both males and females grow antlers, and the males drop theirs in winter, so Santa's team is probably female.
Things Santa needs on Christmas Eve.Sack of toys: Santa's bag of toys is magical, delivering to around a billion children, and in older legends it was filled with gifts for good children.
Things Santa needs on Christmas Eve.Red suit: Santa's red suit was popularized in 20th century advertising, notably by Coca-Cola ads in the 1930s, though red robes were drawn earlier.
Things Santa needs on Christmas Eve.Naughty list: The naughty and nice lists come from the 1934 song Santa Claus Is Comin' to Town, which warns that he's making a list and checking it twice.
Things Santa needs on Christmas Eve.Nice list: The nice list is Santa's record of good children, and Saint Nicholas, the real bishop behind the legend, was known for secret gift-giving.
Things Santa needs on Christmas Eve.Rudolph: Rudolph was created in 1939 by Robert L. May for a Montgomery Ward booklet, and he became the ninth reindeer in a 1949 song.
Things Santa needs on Christmas Eve.Black boots: Santa's black boots are part of the look from 19th century illustrations, and Thomas Nast's drawings helped define it.
Things Santa needs on Christmas Eve.Chimney: Santa's chimney entry has its roots in the northern European tradition that gifts came through the smoke hole or hearth.
Things Santa needs on Christmas Eve.Milk and cookies: The tradition of leaving milk and cookies for Santa grew in America during the Great Depression of the 1930s, as a way to teach giving.
Things Santa needs on Christmas Eve.Jingle bells: Jingle Bells was written in 1857 by James Lord Pierpont as a sleigh-riding song, and was not about Christmas at first.
Things Santa needs on Christmas Eve.White beard: Santa's white beard is part of the classic look, and Thomas Nast's 1860s illustrations helped fix it.
Things Santa needs on Christmas Eve.Surfboard: Surfboards fit Christmas only in the southern hemisphere, where summer beaches host Santa on a surfboard, but not on Santa's usual list.
Things Santa needs on Christmas Eve.Lawnmower: A lawnmower is summer gear for cutting grass, and it has no place on a snowy December night.
Things Santa needs on Christmas Eve.Snorkel: A snorkel is for swimming at the surface, and Santa's trip over rooftops in winter has no water.
Things Santa needs on Christmas Eve.Jack-o'-lantern: A jack-o'-lantern is a carved Halloween pumpkin, a tradition from Irish folk tales, and is nothing to do with Christmas.
Things Santa needs on Christmas Eve.Easter basket: An Easter basket is for hunting eggs in spring, a holiday months away from Christmas Eve, and it has no place in Santa's sleigh.
Things Santa needs on Christmas Eve.Cupid's arrow: Cupid's arrow belongs to Valentine's Day in February, and in Roman myth Cupid is the god of love.
Things Santa needs on Christmas Eve.Leprechaun hat: A leprechaun hat is part of St. Patrick's Day on March 17, and leprechauns come from Irish folklore.
Things Santa needs on Christmas Eve.Beach towel: A beach towel is for summer at the shore, though in Australia, where it is warm in December, Santa sometimes wears shorts.
Things Santa needs on Christmas Eve.Witch's broom: A witch's broom belongs to Halloween on October 31, not Christmas, though Santa is occasionally said to have swept soot from the chimney.
Things Santa needs on Christmas Eve.Tax return: A tax return isn't Christmas-related, and in the United States the filing deadline falls in mid-April, far from December.
Things Santa needs on Christmas Eve.Bathing suit: A bathing suit belongs on a summer beach, though in Australia Santa is sometimes shown arriving at the sand.
Things Santa needs on Christmas Eve.Garden hose: A garden hose waters plants in the warm months and has nothing to do with delivering presents.

Absurd things to pack for camping.Grand piano: A concert grand weighs around 1,000 pounds, which is why piano movers use special skids, and it would sink in camp mud.
Absurd things to pack for camping.Chandelier: Chandeliers began as candle holders in medieval times; hanging crystal from a tree branch would be pretty but hardly practical.
Absurd things to pack for camping.Fax machine: Fax machines were patented in the 1840s, long before telephones, and there's nowhere to plug one in at a campsite.
Absurd things to pack for camping.Clawfoot bathtub: Clawfoot tubs of cast iron can weigh several hundred pounds, so hauling one to the woods is a feat of strength.
Absurd things to pack for camping.Waterbed: Waterbeds were popular in the 1970s, and one full of water weighs well over a thousand pounds.
Absurd things to pack for camping.Ball gown: A ball gown can use many yards of fabric, and a hem dragged across dirt and campfire embers would be ruined.
Absurd things to pack for camping.Tuxedo: The tuxedo is named for Tuxedo Park, New York, where it became fashionable in the 1880s. A campfire is not black tie.
Absurd things to pack for camping.Desktop computer: A desktop computer needs mains power, and most campsites have none. Even the monitor alone would defeat the idea of unplugging.
Absurd things to pack for camping.Fine china: Fine china is fired porcelain, and by its very name came from China; one clumsy drop on a rock ends a set.
Absurd things to pack for camping.Ice sculpture: An ice sculpture can melt in an hour or two in warm conditions, so a campsite would turn it into a puddle.
Absurd things to pack for camping.Red carpet: Rolling out a red carpet comes from ancient Greece, where only gods were supposed to walk on crimson; the woods hardly need one.
Absurd things to pack for camping.Tent: A tent is the classic camping shelter, and modern ones weigh little more than a couple of pounds.
Absurd things to pack for camping.Sleeping bag: Sleeping bags with a down fill can be rated for temperatures well below freezing, packing small for a backpack.
Absurd things to pack for camping.Flashlight: A flashlight beats a campfire for finding things at night, and an LED beam can run for many hours on a small battery.
Absurd things to pack for camping.Lantern: Lanterns have lit camps for centuries; some gas versions still use a delicate mesh mantle that glows white-hot.
Absurd things to pack for camping.Matches: Matches in a waterproof container are a smart camp rule, since wet matches are useless when it matters most.
Absurd things to pack for camping.Bug spray: Bug spray with DEET, developed by the US Army in the 1940s, is still a gold-standard mosquito deterrent.
Absurd things to pack for camping.Marshmallows: Marshmallows are a classic campfire treat, and the first marshmallows were made from the sap of a marsh plant by ancient Egyptians.
Absurd things to pack for camping.Compass: A compass works because Earth is a giant magnet; the needle points to magnetic north, a bit off from true north.
Absurd things to pack for camping.Water bottle: A water bottle is everyday kit, and on a hike you may need about half a liter per hour in warm weather.
Absurd things to pack for camping.Hiking boots: Hiking boots are normal camping gear: good ones protect ankles on uneven ground and keep feet dry on wet trails.
Absurd things to pack for camping.Camp stove: A camp stove lets you cook without a fire, handy where fire bans apply, and it boils water quickly.
Absurd things to pack for camping.Pocketknife: A pocketknife, like the Swiss Army knife dating to 1891, is among the most useful camping tools.
Absurd things to pack for camping.First aid kit: A first aid kit is essential outdoors, since help can be hours away from a remote campsite.

Words meaning 'money paid for work'.Wages: Wages are usually paid hourly or weekly, in contrast to a salary, and the word comes from an old French word for a pledge.
Words meaning 'money paid for work'.Pay: Pay is the plain everyday word for what you earn, and a pay stub is where the details are listed.
Words meaning 'money paid for work'.Earnings: Earnings includes all you make from work, and for companies the word means profit, which is a different thing.
Words meaning 'money paid for work'.Stipend: A stipend is a fixed regular payment, often for students or interns, and comes from the Latin stips, a small payment.
Words meaning 'money paid for work'.Remuneration: Remuneration is a formal word that comes from the Latin for to reward, and shows up in contracts and legal documents.
Words meaning 'money paid for work'.Compensation: Compensation can mean pay in a job, though it also means payment for harm, so context matters.
Words meaning 'money paid for work'.Paycheck: A paycheck is a cheque for wages, and the word persists even though most people are paid by direct deposit.
Words meaning 'money paid for work'.Salary: Salary comes from the Latin for salt, and the legend says Roman soldiers were paid in it, though that's disputed.
Words meaning 'money paid for work'.Pay packet: A pay packet is the British word for one's wages, from when pay came in an envelope of cash.
Words meaning 'money paid for work'.Fee: A fee is paid for professional services, such as a lawyer's or a doctor's, rather than as a regular wage.
Words meaning 'money paid for work'.Debt: Debt is money you owe, not money you earn, so it works in the opposite direction.
Words meaning 'money paid for work'.Loan: A loan is borrowed money you must pay back, so it's not pay for work.
Words meaning 'money paid for work'.Tax: A tax is a compulsory payment to the government, and in fact it's taken out of your pay, not part of it.
Words meaning 'money paid for work'.Rent: Rent is paid for the use of property, and money flows from you to the landlord, not for your work.
Words meaning 'money paid for work'.Bill: A bill is a request for payment for goods or services, so you pay it, and don't receive it.
Words meaning 'money paid for work'.Invoice: An invoice is a request for payment sent by a worker or firm, so it asks for pay but is not the pay itself.
Words meaning 'money paid for work'.Mortgage: A mortgage is a loan secured by property, and the word comes from the French for dead pledge.
Words meaning 'money paid for work'.Refund: A refund is money returned for something you bought, so it isn't a payment for work.
Words meaning 'money paid for work'.Fine: A fine is a penalty for breaking a rule, so money goes the other way, and it's not pay.
Words meaning 'money paid for work'.Toll: A toll is a fee for using a road or bridge, and some date back to ancient times.
Words meaning 'money paid for work'.Ransom: A ransom is paid to free a captive, and it's one of the oldest meanings of the word, nothing to do with a job.
Words meaning 'money paid for work'.Change: Change is the coins and notes you get back after paying, not an earning from work.
Words meaning 'money paid for work'.Deposit: A deposit is money put down as security, or placed in a bank, so it's not pay for work.
Words meaning 'money paid for work'.Tuition: Tuition is the fee you pay for teaching, so it's a cost for education and not a wage.

Pokémon types.Fire: Fire-types are strong against Grass, Ice, Bug and Steel, but weak to Water, Ground and Rock. Charmander is a classic example.
Pokémon types.Water: One of the first starter types, Water beats Fire, Ground and Rock, and Squirtle is its famous starter.
Pokémon types.Grass: Grass is the type of Bulbasaur and is weak to many types, including Fire, Ice, Poison, Flying and Bug.
Pokémon types.Electric: Pikachu made Electric the series' mascot type. Electric moves can't affect Ground-types at all.
Pokémon types.Psychic: In the first games, Psychic was absurdly strong, with only Ghost nominally able to hit it, so later games added Dark and Ghost counters.
Pokémon types.Ghost: Ghost was meant to beat Psychic in the original games, but a bug made it do nothing, and the problem was fixed in later generations.
Pokémon types.Dragon: Dragon-types are weak only to Ice, Dragon and Fairy moves, which is partly why Fairy was introduced in 2013.
Pokémon types.Fairy: Added in Generation VI (X and Y) in 2013, Fairy was the first new type in years, created to rein in the Dragon type.
Pokémon types.Steel: Steel arrived in Generation II and resists a huge number of types, while being weak to Fire, Fighting and Ground.
Pokémon types.Ice: Ice is a notable offense type, hitting Dragon, Flying, Ground and Grass for extra damage, yet is defensively fragile.
Pokémon types.Rock: Rock-types such as Onix are tough but vulnerable to Water, Grass, Fighting, Ground and Steel moves.
Pokémon types.Bug: The Bug type is very common early in the games, and its Pokémon like Caterpie evolve unusually quickly.
Pokémon types.Dark: Dark was introduced in Generation II alongside Steel, in part to balance the then-overpowered Psychic type.
Pokémon types.Poison: Poison-types are one of only a few that can hit Fairy for super-effective damage, which helps Fairy balance.
Pokémon types.Wind: Wind isn't a Pokémon type. Air attacks like Gust belong to the Flying type instead.
Pokémon types.Light: No Light type exists; Dark has no direct opposite type, and light-based moves are usually Psychic or Normal.
Pokémon types.Metal: The Steel type was once called 'Metal' in Japan's early planning, but the English name is Steel.
Pokémon types.Sound: Sound moves such as Hyper Voice are classified under Normal, not given their own type; there's no Sound type.
Pokémon types.Wood: There's no Wood type; plant Pokémon are Grass. Wood is a Chinese element, not a Pokémon type.
Pokémon types.Lightning: The type is called Electric, not Lightning, even though Pikachu's famous move Thunderbolt looks like lightning.
Pokémon types.Thunder: Thunder is the name of an Electric-type move, not a type of its own.
Pokémon types.Shadow: Shadow Pokémon appear in Colosseum and XD as a special status, not as a regular type.
Pokémon types.Magic: Magic isn't a type; Fairy took over the whimsical, magical role in Pokémon in 2013.
Pokémon types.Sand: Sand is a weather condition and a move, Sand Attack, not a Pokémon type; those Pokémon are Ground-type.

Real HTML tags.div: Short for division, it's a blank container used to group content and style it, and it's the workhorse of web layout.
Real HTML tags.span: An inline container that does nothing by itself, handy for styling a few words inside a line of text.
Real HTML tags.img: It embeds a picture, and its alt text helps screen readers and shows when the image fails to load.
Real HTML tags.table: Meant for tabular data. Using tables for page layout was common in the 1990s but is now frowned upon.
Real HTML tags.body: Holds everything visible on a page, while the head stays out of sight.
Real HTML tags.head: Holds invisible information such as the title, character set and links to stylesheets rather than visible content.
Real HTML tags.title: Sets the text on the browser tab and in search results, so every page should have one.
Real HTML tags.form: Wraps input fields and sends their data to a server when submitted.
Real HTML tags.button: A clickable control, and inside a form it submits by default unless you give it a different type.
Real HTML tags.video: Added in HTML5 so browsers could play video natively, without plugins such as Flash.
Real HTML tags.audio: Also arriving with HTML5, it plays sound natively, supporting formats like MP3 and Ogg.
Real HTML tags.script: Embeds or links JavaScript, and it has been part of HTML since the 1990s.
Real HTML tags.footer: An HTML5 semantic tag for the closing content of a page or section, like copyright notices and links.
Real HTML tags.photo: Not a tag. Pictures use img, and browsers just ignore unknown tags like this one.
Real HTML tags.words: No such tag exists. Text goes in elements like p or span.
Real HTML tags.page: Not a tag; the html element wraps the whole page.
Real HTML tags.box: Not a tag. A box on a page is usually a div styled through the CSS box model.
Real HTML tags.paragraph: A spelling trap: the tag is just p, not the full word.
Real HTML tags.heading: Headings use h1 through h6, with h1 being the most important.
Real HTML tags.bold: There's no bold tag. You use b, or the more meaningful strong for important text.
Real HTML tags.italic: There's no italic tag. You use i, or em when you mean emphasis.
Real HTML tags.list: Lists use ul, ol and li, not a list tag.
Real HTML tags.row: A trap: table rows use tr, and the cells inside them are td or th, so a plain row tag doesn't exist.
Real HTML tags.column: There are td and th cells, and col exists only to style columns, but no tag named column.

Originally written in French.Les Misérables: Hugo's 1862 epic follows ex-convict Jean Valjean; it is one of the longest novels, and was written in exile.
Originally written in French.Madame Bovary: Flaubert's 1857 novel was put on trial for obscenity, and he was acquitted; he famously said 'Madame Bovary, c'est moi'.
Originally written in French.The Three Musketeers: Dumas wrote it in French, with help from his collaborator Auguste Maquet; the famous motto 'all for one' is really about four men.
Originally written in French.Candide: Voltaire's 1759 satire follows a naive optimist; he wrote it in just a few days and published it under a pseudonym.
Originally written in French.The Stranger: Camus's 1942 novel opens with a famous line about his mother's death, and illustrates the philosophy of the absurd.
Originally written in French.Germinal: Zola's 1885 novel is about a coal miners' strike in northern France, and its title means 'germination'.
Originally written in French.The Little Prince: Saint-Exupéry's 1943 fable is one of the most translated books in the world, after the Bible and the Quran, in over 500 languages.
Originally written in French.Notre-Dame de Paris: Hugo's 1831 novel (known in English as The Hunchback of Notre-Dame) helped spur the restoration of the cathedral.
Originally written in French.Swann's Way: The first volume of Proust's In Search of Lost Time, it contains the famous madeleine scene; Proust paid to have it published.
Originally written in French.Cyrano de Bergerac: Rostand's 1897 play about a poet with a huge nose was inspired by a real 1600s French soldier of the same name.
Originally written in French.Tartuffe: Molière's 1664 comedy about a religious hypocrite was banned by the king for years, because the church found it offensive.
Originally written in French.Phantom of the Opera: Gaston Leroux's 1910 French novel about a masked genius under the Paris Opera inspired Andrew Lloyd Webber's musical.
Originally written in French.Bonjour Tristesse: Françoise Sagan published this at 18, in 1954, and it was an instant scandal and bestseller.
Originally written in French.Don Quixote: Cervantes wrote this in Spanish, in two parts (1605 and 1615); it is considered the first modern novel.
Originally written in French.The Trial: Kafka wrote this German novel about a man arrested without cause; it was published after his death, against his wishes.
Originally written in French.The Metamorphosis: Kafka's tale of Gregor Samsa, who wakes up as a giant insect, was written in German, not French.
Originally written in French.Faust: Goethe's drama about a man who sells his soul took him about 60 years to finish; it is German.
Originally written in French.War and Peace: Tolstoy's Russian epic, not French, is famous for its huge cast of characters.
Originally written in French.The Divine Comedy: Dante's 14th-century poem was written in Italian and is a trip through Hell, Purgatory and Paradise.
Originally written in French.Pinocchio: Collodi's Italian tale of a wooden puppet whose nose grows began as a newspaper serial in 1881.
Originally written in French.The Name of the Rose: Eco's Italian medieval mystery set in a monastery was a bestseller in the 1980s.
Originally written in French.Heidi: Johanna Spyri's tale of a Swiss orphan was written in German, and has been filmed many times.
Originally written in French.Pippi Longstocking: Astrid Lindgren's Swedish red-braided heroine is the strongest girl in the world.
Originally written in French.Siddhartha: Hesse's tale of a spiritual seeker in India was written in German, not French.

Books by Roald Dahl.Matilda: Published in 1988, this tale of a bookish girl with telekinetic powers became a hit stage musical from the Royal Shakespeare Company in 2010.
Books by Roald Dahl.The BFG: The Big Friendly Giant catches dreams in jars and blows them into children's bedrooms. Dahl dedicated the book to his late daughter Olivia.
Books by Roald Dahl.The Witches: In this 1983 tale witches wear wigs over bald heads, and the boy hero is turned into a mouse and, unusually, stays one for good.
Books by Roald Dahl.Fantastic Mr Fox: Mr Fox outwits three farmers named Boggis, Bunce and Bean. Wes Anderson turned it into a stop-motion film in 2009.
Books by Roald Dahl.The Twits: Mr Twit's beard hides old meals, and the horrid couple are finally defeated by the monkeys they kept caged.
Books by Roald Dahl.Esio Trot: A shy man woos Mrs Silver by pretending to shrink her pet tortoise with a spell. The title is simply 'tortoise' spelled backwards.
Books by Roald Dahl.Boy: Not fiction: Dahl's memoir of his childhood recalls testing new chocolates for Cadbury as a schoolboy, a seed of Charlie and the Chocolate Factory.
Books by Roald Dahl.Going Solo: The sequel to Boy, this memoir covers Dahl's years in East Africa and his time as an RAF fighter pilot, including a crash in the Libyan desert.
Books by Roald Dahl.Revolting Rhymes: Dahl's 1982 verse retellings twist fairy tales: Red Riding Hood shoots the wolf and wears him as a coat.
Books by Roald Dahl.The Magic Finger: A girl's pointing finger turns a hunting family into winged creatures while ducks take over their house. It is one of Dahl's shortest books.
Books by Roald Dahl.The Gruffalo: Julia Donaldson and Axel Scheffler's 1999 picture book: a clever mouse invents a monster that turns out to be real. Not a Dahl.
Books by Roald Dahl.Holes: Louis Sachar's 1998 novel follows a boy forced to dig holes at Camp Green Lake. It won the Newbery Medal.
Books by Roald Dahl.Wonder: R. J. Palacio's 2012 novel follows Auggie, a boy with a facial difference starting school, told by several narrators.
Books by Roald Dahl.Coraline: Neil Gaiman's 2002 dark fantasy about a girl and her button-eyed Other Mother is creepy enough to feel Dahl-like, but it isn't.
Books by Roald Dahl.Stuart Little: E. B. White wrote this 1945 tale of a mouse born into a human family before he wrote Charlotte's Web.
Books by Roald Dahl.Charlotte's Web: E. B. White's 1952 classic: Charlotte weaves words like SOME PIG into her web to save Wilbur from the butcher.
Books by Roald Dahl.The Hobbit: Tolkien's 1937 tale grew out of stories he told his own children, and it paved the way for The Lord of the Rings.
Books by Roald Dahl.Mary Poppins: P. L. Travers, an Australian-born writer, created the magical nanny in 1934. She famously disliked Disney's 1964 film version.
Books by Roald Dahl.The Borrowers: Mary Norton's 1952 tale of tiny people living under the floorboards and borrowing from humans won the Carnegie Medal.
Books by Roald Dahl.Pippi Longstocking: Astrid Lindgren invented the super-strong Swedish girl in 1945 to entertain her sick daughter, who named the character.
Books by Roald Dahl.Black Beauty: Anna Sewell's only novel, told by a horse, appeared in 1877, just months before she died. It helped push for kinder treatment of horses.
Books by Roald Dahl.Heidi: Johanna Spyri's 1881 story of a Swiss orphan in the Alps is one of the best-loved children's books ever published.
Books by Roald Dahl.The Secret Garden: Frances Hodgson Burnett's 1911 novel sends orphan Mary Lennox from India to a Yorkshire manor with a hidden, locked garden.
Books by Roald Dahl.Paddington: Michael Bond's marmalade-loving bear from darkest Peru was found at a London station, which gave him his name, in 1958.

Best known as sculptors.Auguste Rodin: The Thinker and The Kiss made him the best-known modern sculptor; The Gates of Hell kept him busy for decades.
Best known as sculptors.Donatello: Florentine who made the first free-standing bronze nude since antiquity with his David around the 1440s.
Best known as sculptors.Bernini: Baroque master who carved The Ecstasy of Saint Teresa, and designed the colonnade around St Peter's Square.
Best known as sculptors.Brâncuși: Romanian-born, he argued with US customs in 1927 over whether his Bird in Space counted as art or a metal item for tax.
Best known as sculptors.Henry Moore: English sculptor known for reclining figures with holes in them, many inspired by Yorkshire hills.
Best known as sculptors.Giacometti: The Swiss sculptor of stretched, spindly figures; one of his Walking Man casts sold for over $100 million.
Best known as sculptors.Louise Bourgeois: Her giant spider Maman, over nine meters tall, stands outside several museums worldwide.
Best known as sculptors.Barbara Hepworth: English sculptor of pierced forms who lived in St Ives; her Single Form stands outside the UN.
Best known as sculptors.Antony Gormley: His Angel of the North, a steel figure in Gateshead from 1998, has a wingspan like a jumbo jet.
Best known as sculptors.Canova: Italian Neoclassical master whose marble Psyche Revived by Cupid's Kiss looks soft as flesh.
Best known as sculptors.Phidias: Greek sculptor of the Parthenon; his statue of Zeus at Olympia counted among the Seven Wonders.
Best known as sculptors.Claude Monet: A French painter of Water Lilies, famed for Impressionism, who never made sculpture.
Best known as sculptors.Van Gogh: Painted about 2,000 works in roughly a decade, nearly all paintings and drawings, so he is not known as a sculptor.
Best known as sculptors.Rembrandt: A Dutch painter and etcher famed for portraits and self-portraits; he left sculpture to others.
Best known as sculptors.Vermeer: Painter of light-filled Delft interiors; only about three dozen paintings are attributed to him.
Best known as sculptors.J. M. W. Turner: A landscape and storm painter who left thousands of works to the British nation; he never worked in stone or bronze.
Best known as sculptors.John Constable: His Hay Wain is a beloved English landscape painting; he painted skies in oil sketches, not sculpture.
Best known as sculptors.Frida Kahlo: A Mexican painter, best known for self-portraits; her small, intense canvases are paintings, not sculptures.
Best known as sculptors.Jackson Pollock: The American drip painter, who poured paint onto canvases laid on the floor; his fame is in painting.
Best known as sculptors.Mark Rothko: A color-field painter, known for floating rectangles of glowing color; a painter, not a sculptor.
Best known as sculptors.Gustav Klimt: An Austrian Symbolist painter famed for gold-leaf works like The Kiss, a painting not a sculpture.
Best known as sculptors.Botticelli: An early Renaissance Florentine painter of The Birth of Venus and Primavera, not a sculptor.
Best known as sculptors.Caravaggio: An Italian Baroque painter known for dramatic light and a violent life, not for sculpture.
Best known as sculptors.Raphael: An Italian painter and architect, who died at 37 after a busy Vatican career; no sculptures to his name.

Abstract Expressionist painters.Jackson Pollock: He poured paint onto canvases laid on the floor, which led Time magazine to nickname him "Jack the Dripper".
Abstract Expressionist painters.Mark Rothko: His glowing, soft-edged color rectangles were meant to be seen up close, and he withdrew from a restaurant mural commission.
Abstract Expressionist painters.Willem de Kooning: Dutch-born, his Woman series shocked fellow abstractionists by returning to the human figure in the 1950s.
Abstract Expressionist painters.Franz Kline: His slashing black-and-white brushstrokes look like girders or calligraphy, and some are painted on huge canvases.
Abstract Expressionist painters.Lee Krasner: She cut up her own old paintings to make collages after Pollock's death in 1956, and became a major artist.
Abstract Expressionist painters.Barnett Newman: His "zips", thin vertical lines slicing through huge fields of color, are the signature of his work.
Abstract Expressionist painters.Clyfford Still: His jagged, flame-like color fields grew from his withdrawal from the New York art world, and his work fills a Denver museum.
Abstract Expressionist painters.Helen Frankenthaler: She invented soak-stain painting, pouring thinned paint into raw canvas, inspiring the Color Field movement.
Abstract Expressionist painters.Robert Motherwell: His Elegy to the Spanish Republic series of black ovals runs to well over a hundred paintings.
Abstract Expressionist painters.Joan Mitchell: She painted vast canvases of dense brushstrokes, many recalling landscapes, and lived in Vetheuil, France.
Abstract Expressionist painters.Arshile Gorky: Armenian-born, he bridged Surrealism and abstraction, and influenced Pollock and de Kooning before his death in 1948.
Abstract Expressionist painters.Andy Warhol: A leading Pop artist who came after the movement, and turned soup cans and celebrities into art.
Abstract Expressionist painters.Roy Lichtenstein: He enlarged comic panels with Ben-Day dots, a cool Pop style opposite the gestural mood of Abstract Expressionism.
Abstract Expressionist painters.Salvador Dalí: A Spanish Surrealist famous for melting clocks, and not part of the New York School at all.
Abstract Expressionist painters.René Magritte: The Belgian Surrealist behind The Treachery of Images ("This is not a pipe"), part of a different movement.
Abstract Expressionist painters.Claude Monet: An Impressionist whose "Impression, Sunrise" gave that movement its name, decades before 1940s New York.
Abstract Expressionist painters.Edward Hopper: A realist painter of lonely Americana, defiantly figurative, who stayed outside the abstract movement.
Abstract Expressionist painters.Norman Rockwell: Illustrator of Saturday Evening Post covers, whose pictures told clear stories, the opposite of abstraction.
Abstract Expressionist painters.Grant Wood: A Regionalist who painted American Gothic, so he was a figurative artist, nothing like the abstract New Yorkers.
Abstract Expressionist painters.Andrew Wyeth: A realist famed for Christina's World, painted in tempera, and the opposite of gestural abstraction.
Abstract Expressionist painters.Piet Mondrian: A Dutch geometric abstractionist who moved to New York in 1940 but died in 1944, before the movement peaked.
Abstract Expressionist painters.Keith Haring: His bold, outlined figures came from 1980s street culture and Pop, not from the 1940s and 50s New York School.
Abstract Expressionist painters.Frida Kahlo: A Mexican painter who rejected the Surrealist label, and is not a part of the New York School.
Abstract Expressionist painters.Gustav Klimt: An Austrian Symbolist famed for gold leaf, who died in 1918, decades before Abstract Expressionism began.
