Fantasy book series.Harry Potter: Rowling's first book was turned down by about a dozen publishers before Bloomsbury took it, reportedly thanks to an eight-year-old's enthusiasm.
Fantasy book series.Discworld: Terry Pratchett's flat world rides on four elephants standing on the shell of a giant turtle, A'Tuin, and he wrote over 40 books there.
Fantasy book series.Earthsea: Ursula K. Le Guin's 1968 wizard school on Roke predates Hogwarts, and magic works by knowing the true names of things.
Fantasy book series.The Wheel of Time: Robert Jordan died before finishing it, so Brandon Sanderson completed the last three of its fourteen huge volumes from Jordan's notes.
Fantasy book series.Percy Jackson: Rick Riordan first told these as bedtime stories to his son, who has ADHD and dyslexia, like his hero Percy.
Fantasy book series.His Dark Materials: Philip Pullman took the title from Milton's Paradise Lost; the first book is called The Golden Compass in North America.
Fantasy book series.The Witcher: These began as Polish short stories by Andrzej Sapkowski, long before the video games made the monster hunter Geralt a global name.
Fantasy book series.Redwall: Brian Jacques first wrote it for pupils at a Liverpool school for the blind, where he delivered milk, which is why the feasts are so vivid.
Fantasy book series.Mistborn: Brandon Sanderson's heroes swallow bits of metal and 'burn' them inside, each metal giving a different power.
Fantasy book series.Artemis Fowl: Eoin Colfer's hero is a twelve-year-old Irish criminal mastermind who plots to kidnap a fairy and ransom her for gold.
Fantasy book series.Inkheart: Cornelia Funke's German original has characters who can read people out of books, and the hero Mo is nicknamed Silvertongue.
Fantasy book series.Shannara: Terry Brooks's 1977 debut, The Sword of Shannara, was an early fantasy bestseller, heavily inspired by Tolkien.
Fantasy book series.Narnia: C. S. Lewis's seven books began with a mental image of a faun carrying an umbrella and parcels in a snowy wood.
Fantasy book series.Dune: This is science fiction, not fantasy: Frank Herbert's desert planet Arrakis is the only source of the spice that powers interstellar travel.
Fantasy book series.Foundation: Asimov's saga is science fiction; its 'psychohistory' predicts a galactic empire's fall, and he modelled it on Gibbon's Roman history.
Fantasy book series.The Hunger Games: Suzanne Collins's dystopian novels fuse reality TV with war coverage, and the arena echoes the Greek myth of Theseus.
Fantasy book series.Divergent: Veronica Roth wrote this dystopia, set in a walled-off future Chicago, while still a university student.
Fantasy book series.Nancy Drew: Nancy Drew's author 'Carolyn Keene' never existed: it was a pen name for several ghostwriters, starting in 1930.
Fantasy book series.Hardy Boys: Franklin W. Dixon, credited as the author of these mysteries, is another house pen name used by many ghostwriters.
Fantasy book series.Jack Reacher: Lee Child is a Briton who set his tough thriller hero in America, where there is no magic, just fists and logic.
Fantasy book series.The Expanse: This science fiction series is by 'James S. A. Corey', a pen name shared by Daniel Abraham and Ty Franck.
Fantasy book series.Goosebumps: R. L. Stine's horror series for children has sold hundreds of millions of copies worldwide, but its monsters are horror, not fantasy.
Fantasy book series.Captain Underpants: Dav Pilkey's comic novels about two pranksters and their superhero headmaster are humor, and are often among the most challenged books in US libraries.
Fantasy book series.Maze Runner: James Dashner's teens wake in a glade ringed by a deadly shifting maze: dystopian science fiction, not fantasy.

Sticky things.Honey: Honey is so sticky and low in water that it never spoils; edible honey was found in Egyptian tombs thousands of years old.
Sticky things.Glue: Superglue was found by accident in 1942 when a scientist hoping for clear plastic gun sights found something that bonded everything.
Sticky things.Duct tape: It was first made during World War II to seal ammunition cases, and was called 'duck tape' for the cotton duck fabric.
Sticky things.Maple syrup: It takes roughly 40 liters of sap to boil down to one liter of syrup, which is why it's so sticky and expensive.
Sticky things.Chewed gum: The gum base is made of synthetic polymers that don't dissolve, which is why it clings to shoes and stays for years.
Sticky things.Molasses: Molasses is the thick, dark syrup left after sugar crystals are removed, and in 1919 a Boston tank burst, flooding streets in a deadly wave.
Sticky things.Tree sap: Sap hardens into amber over millions of years, and insects trapped in it are preserved as fossils.
Sticky things.Caramel: Caramel forms when sugar is heated above about 170 degrees Celsius, and that browning gives it its stickiness and flavor.
Sticky things.Sticky note: The Post-it's weak glue was a failed experiment at 3M in 1968, and it took years to find a use for it.
Sticky things.Flypaper: Sticky strips coated with adhesive have trapped flies since the 1800s, and they lure insects with sweet-smelling bait.
Sticky things.Peanut butter: It's so sticky that dogs love licking it, and eating a spoonful can make your mouth feel glued.
Sticky things.Spider web: Spider silk is stronger than steel by weight, and orb weavers coat their capture threads with sticky droplets.
Sticky things.Magnet: Magnets attract only iron-like metals, and they don't stick to wood or skin, which keeps them out of this list.
Sticky things.Sand: Sand sticks when wet, which is why sandcastles work, but dry sand slides off.
Sticky things.Feather: Feathers are light and can stick if damp, but they are not adhesive.
Sticky things.Marble: Marbles are smooth glass spheres that roll rather than stick.
Sticky things.Water: Water clings to surfaces through surface tension, but it doesn't remain stuck, and it simply flows.
Sticky things.Glass: Glass is smooth and non-porous, so little sticks to it, which is why windows are easy to clean.
Sticky things.Ice cube: An ice cube can stick to a wet finger, but only because the moisture freezes, not because of any glue.
Sticky things.Silk scarf: Silk is slippery and smooth, which makes it the opposite of sticky.
Sticky things.Teflon pan: Teflon is one of the slipperiest substances known, and was invented in 1938 and used in non-stick pans.
Sticky things.Bar of soap: Soap is slippery when wet, and that is how it loosens grease from skin.
Sticky things.Paper towel: Paper towels absorb liquid but they do not stick to anything.
Sticky things.Pebble: A pebble is a smooth, hard stone that rolls rather than sticks.

Things with tails.Comet: A comet's tail always points away from the Sun, pushed by solar wind and radiation, even when the comet is heading outward.
Things with tails.Kite: A kite's tail adds drag and weight at the back, which keeps the nose pointed into the wind so it doesn't tumble.
Things with tails.Airplane: The tail fin of a plane, called the empennage, steadies it, and airline logos are often painted on it.
Things with tails.Dog: Dogs wag their tails differently depending on mood, and a wag to the right is often linked to positive feelings.
Things with tails.Tadpole: A tadpole's tail is absorbed into its body as it becomes a frog, and the tail's material is reused, not discarded.
Things with tails.Lizard: Many lizards can drop their tail to escape a predator, and it often wriggles on to distract it, and later grows back.
Things with tails.Peacock: The long "tail" of a peacock is actually upper tail coverts, and it can have about 150 feathers.
Things with tails.Coin: The "tails" side of a coin is called the reverse, and flipping one is not quite 50-50, since it favours the starting side slightly.
Things with tails.Mermaid: Mermaids are drawn with a fish tail from the waist down, and the legend includes the Syrian goddess Atargatis.
Things with tails.Horse: A horse's tail swats flies and also signals mood, and it has no bone through most of its length, just hair.
Things with tails.Squirrel: A squirrel's bushy tail helps with balance and acts as a blanket in cold weather.
Things with tails.Kangaroo: The tail acts as a fifth leg when it walks slowly, and as a prop when it stands upright.
Things with tails.Frog: A trap: adult frogs have no tail, though tadpoles do, and the tail is absorbed during the change.
Things with tails.Gorilla: Gorillas, like all apes, have no tail, which is what sets them apart from monkeys.
Things with tails.Chimpanzee: Chimps are apes, and apes have no tails, which is one of the ways to tell them apart from monkeys.
Things with tails.Spider: A spider has a body in two parts and no tail, only spinnerets at the back for spinning silk.
Things with tails.Jellyfish: Jellyfish have a bell and trailing tentacles, which can sting, but no tail.
Things with tails.Starfish: Starfish have arms, usually five, and can regrow a lost one, but they have no tail.
Things with tails.Octopus: An octopus has eight arms and no tail, and three hearts and blue blood.
Things with tails.Snail: A snail has a muscular foot and a shell, and no tail, although the end of its foot looks like one.
Things with tails.Orangutan: Orangutans are apes, and have no tail, and their name means "person of the forest" in Malay.
Things with tails.Ladybug: Ladybugs are beetles and have no tail, just a hard rear shell cover.
Things with tails.Butterfly: Butterflies have no tail, though swallowtail species have tail-like extensions on their hindwings.
Things with tails.Hot air balloon: A hot air balloon has an envelope and basket, and nothing that looks like a tail.

Animals with six legs.Ant: Ants are among the most successful insects, with over 14,000 species, and a colony works as a single superorganism with a queen.
Animals with six legs.Bee: A honeybee's wings beat around 200 times a second, which creates the buzz, and a worker visits thousands of flowers in a day.
Animals with six legs.Beetle: Beetles are the largest group of animals, with roughly 400,000 known species, and the geneticist J.B.S. Haldane reputedly quipped that God had an inordinate fondness for them.
Animals with six legs.Butterfly: A caterpillar has six true legs and several fleshy prolegs, but an adult butterfly keeps just six, like all insects, and tastes with its feet.
Animals with six legs.Grasshopper: A grasshopper's powerful back legs let it jump over twenty times its body length, and it hears using ears on its abdomen.
Animals with six legs.Ladybug: Ladybugs release a smelly yellow fluid from their leg joints to put off predators, and bright red warns birds that they taste bad.
Animals with six legs.Dragonfly: Dragonflies are ancient insects, with relatives that had wingspans over 70 centimeters, and their six legs are used mainly to catch prey in mid-air.
Animals with six legs.Cockroach: Cockroaches can live for a week or more without their heads, because their bodies breathe through small holes along the sides.
Animals with six legs.Mosquito: Only female mosquitoes bite, since they need blood protein for their eggs, while males sip nectar, and all have six legs.
Animals with six legs.Termite: Termites build towering mounds with ventilation, and some African ones reach several meters, and they are more closely related to cockroaches than to ants.
Animals with six legs.Housefly: A housefly tastes with its feet, and it can walk upside down on a ceiling using sticky pads on each of its six legs.
Animals with six legs.Cricket: Male crickets chirp by rubbing their wings together, and the pace of the chirps rises with warmth, which is the basis of Dolbear's law.
Animals with six legs.Praying mantis: Mantises hold their front pair of legs folded like praying hands, ready to snap out at prey, and they can swivel their heads to look over a shoulder.
Animals with six legs.Spider: Spiders have eight legs, so they fail here, and unlike insects they have two body segments, not three.
Animals with six legs.Scorpion: Scorpions are arachnids with eight legs, plus two pincers and a tail, and some glow under ultraviolet light.
Animals with six legs.Tick: Adult ticks are arachnids with eight legs, though the larvae hatch with six legs and gain two more after their first molt.
Animals with six legs.Crab: A crab has ten legs, counting its claws, which makes it a decapod, a word that means ten feet.
Animals with six legs.Centipede: Centipedes have one pair of legs per body segment, with some species having over 100 legs, so far from six.
Animals with six legs.Millipede: Despite the name meaning a thousand feet, millipedes have two pairs per segment, and the record holder has about 1,300 legs.
Animals with six legs.Lobster: A lobster is a crustacean with ten legs, including its claws, and it can live several decades.
Animals with six legs.Octopus: An octopus has eight arms, not six legs, and three hearts, with blue blood.
Animals with six legs.Starfish: Most sea stars have five arms, with tube feet in rows beneath, and have no legs in the usual sense.
Animals with six legs.Dust mite: Dust mites are tiny arachnids with eight legs, and they thrive in bedding, feeding on flakes of skin.
Animals with six legs.Snail: A snail has no legs at all, but moves on one muscular foot over a trail of slime.

Things that harden by drying not cooling.Clay: Air-dry clay hardens as water evaporates, but pottery clay needs firing to become permanently hard.
Things that harden by drying not cooling.Wet cement: Cement actually hardens through a chemical reaction with water called hydration, which even works underwater.
Things that harden by drying not cooling.Glue: Many white glues set as their water evaporates, leaving a tough plastic film behind.
Things that harden by drying not cooling.Nail polish: Nail polish dries as its solvent evaporates, leaving a hard film of nitrocellulose.
Things that harden by drying not cooling.Plaster: Plaster of Paris sets after mixing with water through a heat-giving reaction, and was used for casts.
Things that harden by drying not cooling.Paint: Latex paint dries as water evaporates and the particles fuse into a film, while oil paint hardens by reacting with oxygen.
Things that harden by drying not cooling.Mud: Mud hardens as water evaporates, leaving cracked earth, and mud bricks have been used for around 10,000 years.
Things that harden by drying not cooling.Papier-mâché: Papier-mâché means chewed paper in French, and it becomes rigid as the paste dries.
Things that harden by drying not cooling.Royal icing: Royal icing is egg white and sugar, and it dries rock hard, which is why it holds gingerbread houses together.
Things that harden by drying not cooling.Mortar: Mortar sets by evaporation and a slow reaction with carbon dioxide, and the ancient Romans' version has lasted millennia.
Things that harden by drying not cooling.Play-Doh: Play-Doh began as a wallpaper cleaner and dries hard if left out.
Things that harden by drying not cooling.Butter: Butter hardens when cooled, since it's a fat that solidifies at lower temperatures.
Things that harden by drying not cooling.Melted chocolate: Chocolate sets as the cocoa butter crystallizes while cooling, and tempering controls the shine.
Things that harden by drying not cooling.Candle wax: Candle wax hardens when it cools below its melting point, and doesn't dry.
Things that harden by drying not cooling.Ice: Ice forms by freezing at 0 degrees Celsius, which is cooling and not drying.
Things that harden by drying not cooling.Jell-O: Jell-O sets by cooling, as gelatin chains link into a gel.
Things that harden by drying not cooling.Lava: Lava hardens as it cools into rock, and it takes years for thick flows to solidify fully.
Things that harden by drying not cooling.Caramel: Caramel hardens as the sugar cools, and it turns brittle when cooked to a higher temperature.
Things that harden by drying not cooling.Fudge: Fudge sets as the sugar crystals form while cooling, and beating it makes the crystals small and smooth.
Things that harden by drying not cooling.Cotton shirt: A wet cotton shirt dries soft, and it hardens only if starched.
Things that harden by drying not cooling.Bath towel: A towel dries soft or crunchy, and it doesn't harden like a glue.
Things that harden by drying not cooling.Sand: Sand dries into loose grains and not a solid.
Things that harden by drying not cooling.Feather: A feather stays the same whether wet or dry.
Things that harden by drying not cooling.Hair: Hair dries but stays flexible, unless you add gel, which stiffens as it dries.

Parts of a car.Steering wheel: Early cars were steered with a tiller, and the round steering wheel arrived around 1900, and the first one is credited to Panhard et Levassor.
Parts of a car.Bumper: Bumpers were once purely decorative, and US rules in the 1970s required 5 mph impact bumpers, which is why some of those cars looked heavy.
Parts of a car.Windshield: Modern windshields are laminated, with a plastic layer between two sheets of glass, so they crack but hold together.
Parts of a car.Hood: In British English this part is called the bonnet, and the front hood of most cars covers the engine and crumple zone.
Parts of a car.Trunk: The trunk gets its name from early luggage trunks strapped to the car's rear, and British English calls it the boot.
Parts of a car.Gearbox: A gearbox lets the engine run efficiently at different speeds, and modern ones can have eight or more forward gears.
Parts of a car.Exhaust: A car's exhaust carries burned gases away and includes a catalytic converter that turns toxic gases into less harmful ones.
Parts of a car.Radiator: A car radiator works with coolant, and it keeps the engine from overheating, since much of the fuel's energy becomes heat.
Parts of a car.Spark plug: A spark plug fires thousands of times a minute to ignite fuel, and it needs a voltage of many thousands of volts.
Parts of a car.Dashboard: The word dashboard began on horse-drawn carriages, where it was a board that shielded riders from mud dashed up by hooves.
Parts of a car.Clutch: The clutch disconnects the engine from the wheels so you can change gears, and it's why manual drivers press a third pedal.
Parts of a car.Axle: The axle is the shaft that carries the wheels, and the wheel and axle are among the oldest inventions, dating to about 3500 BC.
Parts of a car.Muffler: The muffler quiets exhaust noise, and in British English it's called a silencer; it works by bouncing sound waves around inside.
Parts of a car.Hubcap: Hubcaps cover the center of the wheel, and they were originally made to keep dirt out of the wheel bearings.
Parts of a car.Handlebar: Handlebars steer bicycles and motorcycles, and cars use a steering wheel, so this part trips people up.
Parts of a car.Kickstand: A kickstand props up a bike or motorcycle, since two-wheelers can't stand upright on their own, and cars stay up on four wheels.
Parts of a car.Rudder: A rudder steers a boat or aircraft by deflecting flow, while cars steer by turning their front wheels instead.
Parts of a car.Propeller: A propeller spins to push a ship or plane through fluid, and cars are driven by their wheels, so it doesn't fit.
Parts of a car.Mast: A mast holds up a ship's sails, and cars never need one, though some have a short antenna that looks like a mast.
Parts of a car.Keel: The keel is the boat's backbone along the bottom, and it keeps the vessel from tipping or sliding sideways.
Parts of a car.Saddle: A saddle is the seat on a horse or a bicycle, and a car has bucket or bench seats, so this one belongs elsewhere.
Parts of a car.Sail: Sails catch the wind to move a boat, which a car doesn't need, though some experimental cars have run on wind power.
Parts of a car.Fuselage: The fuselage is an aircraft's main body, which holds crew and cargo, while cars use the word chassis and body instead.
Parts of a car.Periscope: A periscope lets submarine crews see above the surface, using angled mirrors or prisms, and cars use mirrors instead.

Famous ships, not planes or trains.Titanic: The RMS Titanic hit an iceberg in April 1912, and a novel, Futility, written 14 years earlier eerily described a ship called Titan sinking the same way.
Famous ships, not planes or trains.Mayflower: In 1620 it carried about 100 Pilgrims to America, and it was aiming for the Hudson River area but landed far north at Cape Cod.
Famous ships, not planes or trains.Bismarck: This German battleship sank HMS Hood in 1941 in minutes, and was itself sunk days later after a huge chase.
Famous ships, not planes or trains.Lusitania: The British liner was torpedoed by a German U-boat in 1915, and its sinking helped push the US toward joining World War I.
Famous ships, not planes or trains.Queen Mary: The Cunard ocean liner, launched in 1934, now sits as a hotel and museum in Long Beach, California.
Famous ships, not planes or trains.Santa Maria: Columbus's flagship in 1492 ran aground off Hispaniola on Christmas Day, so he left timbers to build a fort.
Famous ships, not planes or trains.HMS Victory: Nelson's flagship at Trafalgar in 1805 is still in commission, the oldest naval ship in the world, and sits in dry dock in Portsmouth.
Famous ships, not planes or trains.Cutty Sark: A fast 1869 tea clipper that is preserved in Greenwich, London, and its name comes from a short shirt worn by a witch in a Burns poem.
Famous ships, not planes or trains.HMS Beagle: Charles Darwin sailed on it from 1831 to 1836, and observations on the voyage including the Galapagos shaped his theory of evolution.
Famous ships, not planes or trains.Mary Rose: Henry VIII's warship sank in 1545 in view of the king, and was raised in 1982 with thousands of Tudor artifacts.
Famous ships, not planes or trains.Endurance: Shackleton's ship was crushed by Antarctic ice in 1915, and the whole crew survived, and the wreck was found in 2022.
Famous ships, not planes or trains.Orient Express: A luxury train, not a ship, linking Paris and Istanbul, and it inspired Agatha Christie's famous murder mystery.
Famous ships, not planes or trains.Flying Scotsman: A famous steam locomotive from 1923, and in 1934 it was the first to be officially clocked at 100 mph.
Famous ships, not planes or trains.Enola Gay: The Boeing B-29 bomber that dropped the atomic bomb on Hiroshima in 1945, named for the pilot's mother, so it's a plane.
Famous ships, not planes or trains.Spirit of St. Louis: Charles Lindbergh's plane flew solo across the Atlantic in 1927 over 33 hours, so it is not a ship.
Famous ships, not planes or trains.Hindenburg: A German airship that burned in 1937 at Lakehurst, and it's a zeppelin rather than a seagoing ship.
Famous ships, not planes or trains.Concorde: The supersonic jet flew at twice the speed of sound, and so is a plane.
Famous ships, not planes or trains.Air Force One: The call sign of any aircraft carrying the US president, which makes it a plane, not a ship.
Famous ships, not planes or trains.Mallard: A British steam locomotive that set the world steam record of 126 mph in 1938, so a train, not a ship.
Famous ships, not planes or trains.Hogwarts Express: The fictional steam train in Harry Potter is a train, and the real engine used in films is a GWR Hall class.
Famous ships, not planes or trains.Spruce Goose: Howard Hughes' giant wooden flying boat flew only once, in 1947, for about a mile, so it's a plane.
Famous ships, not planes or trains.Memphis Belle: A B-17 bomber that became famous for surviving 25 missions in WWII, so it's an aircraft.
Famous ships, not planes or trains.Shinkansen: The Japanese bullet train that began in 1964, so a train, not a ship.
Famous ships, not planes or trains.Red Baron: The nickname of German WWI fighter ace Manfred von Richthofen, who flew a red Fokker triplane, and who is a pilot, not a ship.

Things you'd find in a wizard's tower.Spellbook: Spellbooks, or grimoires, were real medieval texts, and some contain instructions for rituals.
Things you'd find in a wizard's tower.Cauldron: The cauldron is a witch's cooking pot, and real iron cauldrons were used in Iron Age feasts.
Things you'd find in a wizard's tower.Crystal ball: Crystal balls were often made of polished quartz or beryl, and a fortune teller would gaze into one, a practice called scrying.
Things you'd find in a wizard's tower.Wand: The wand has been a symbol of magic for centuries, and the Greek god Hermes carried a similar staff.
Things you'd find in a wizard's tower.Potion: Potion comes from Latin "potio", a drink, and the same root gave us "poison".
Things you'd find in a wizard's tower.Broomstick: The idea of witches on broomsticks comes from medieval accounts of witches' "flying ointment".
Things you'd find in a wizard's tower.Pointy hat: The pointed hat associated with wizards has been a symbol since the Middle Ages.
Things you'd find in a wizard's tower.Scroll: Scrolls were used for writing before books, and the Dead Sea Scrolls are over 2,000 years old.
Things you'd find in a wizard's tower.Hourglass: An hourglass measures time using sand, and it was widely used on ships to keep time.
Things you'd find in a wizard's tower.Candle: Before electricity, scholars and wizards worked by candlelight, and beeswax candles burned cleaner than tallow.
Things you'd find in a wizard's tower.Quill: Quills were usually made from goose feathers, and typically came from the left wing for right-handed writers.
Things you'd find in a wizard's tower.Microwave: A microwave is a modern appliance, invented in the 1940s after a radar engineer's chocolate bar melted.
Things you'd find in a wizard's tower.Laptop: A laptop needs electricity and Wi-Fi, which a medieval wizard's tower would not have.
Things you'd find in a wizard's tower.Treadmill: The treadmill was originally invented as a prison punishment in the 1800s.
Things you'd find in a wizard's tower.Toaster: A toaster needs electricity; the first electric one dates from 1893.
Things you'd find in a wizard's tower.Vacuum cleaner: A vacuum cleaner is a modern invention, first made in the early 1900s, and a wizard would use a broom.
Things you'd find in a wizard's tower.Smartphone: A smartphone needs a network, and a medieval wizard's tower wouldn't have one.
Things you'd find in a wizard's tower.Wi-Fi router: A Wi-Fi router is a modern device from the 1990s, so it doesn't belong in a wizard's tower.
Things you'd find in a wizard's tower.Television: The television, invented in the 1920s, is far too modern for a wizard's tower.
Things you'd find in a wizard's tower.Hairdryer: Hairdryers came about in the late 1800s, and handheld electric ones arrived in the 1920s; a wizard would need a spell.
Things you'd find in a wizard's tower.Dishwasher: The dishwasher was invented by Josephine Cochrane in the 1880s, and a wizard would use a spell instead.
Things you'd find in a wizard's tower.Electric guitar: The electric guitar dates from the 1930s, and a wizard would more likely play a lute.
Things you'd find in a wizard's tower.Lawn mower: The lawn mower was invented in 1830 by Edwin Budding, and a wizard's tower is more likely surrounded by overgrown weeds.
Things you'd find in a wizard's tower.Jet ski: A jet ski is a modern water craft, and has no place in a wizard's tower.

Car models named after animals.Bronco: Ford's off-roader, named for an untamed horse, came out in 1966 and returned in 2021 after a 25-year break.
Car models named after animals.Panda: Fiat's boxy little car, designed by Giorgetto Giugiaro, was launched in 1980 and is named for the black-and-white bear.

Car models named after animals.Fiesta: Ford's small hatchback is named for a Spanish festival, and it was produced from 1976 until 2023.

Car models named after animals.Corvette: Chevrolet's sports car is named for a small warship, not an animal, even though its Sting Ray cousin is.

Things a ship's captain might shout.Ahoy: Alexander Graham Bell reportedly suggested 'ahoy' as the telephone greeting, but 'hello' won out.
Things a ship's captain might shout.Land ho: A lookout's cry on first sighting land; Columbus's crew heard 'Tierra!' from the Pinta in 1492.
Things a ship's captain might shout.Avast: Avast means 'stop' or 'hold fast', from Dutch 'hou vast', and is a pirate-film staple.
Things a ship's captain might shout.All hands on deck: The call for every crew member to help in an emergency, now used on land for any big job.
Things a ship's captain might shout.Man overboard: At sea it's a drill: someone shouts, throws a lifebuoy, and the ship turns to rescue them, which takes real time.
Things a ship's captain might shout.Abandon ship: In a sinking, 'abandon ship' orders everyone into lifeboats, and a captain traditionally leaves last.
Things a ship's captain might shout.Anchors aweigh: It means the anchor has just been lifted off the seabed, and it is also the US Navy's song.
Things a ship's captain might shout.Full speed ahead: A telegraph on a ship's bridge sent this order to the engine room using a dial, long before radios.
Things a ship's captain might shout.Hard to port: 'Port' replaced 'larboard' because it sounded too like 'starboard' in a storm; the helm turns left.
Things a ship's captain might shout.Drop anchor: Anchors grip the seabed, and ships usually let out chain several times as long as the water is deep.
Things a ship's captain might shout.Hoist the sails: Sails go up with halyards, and the order means the ship is ready to get under way.
Things a ship's captain might shout.Timber: A lumberjack's warning shout as a felled tree begins to fall, so people nearby can get clear.
Things a ship's captain might shout.Olé: Spanish crowds shout it at bullfights and flamenco, and some say it descends from Arabic 'wa-llah'.
Things a ship's captain might shout.Checkmate: From Persian 'shah mat', roughly 'the king is helpless'; a chess game ends when the king can't escape.
Things a ship's captain might shout.Bingo: Bingo started as an Italian lottery in the 1500s, and in the US was once called 'beano'.
Things a ship's captain might shout.Touchdown: A touchdown scores six points in American football, a cry from the crowd rather than the bridge.
Things a ship's captain might shout.Encore: It's French for 'again', but French audiences don't actually shout 'encore'; they say 'bis'.
Things a ship's captain might shout.Cheese: Photographers say it because the 'ee' sound pulls your lips into a smile, a trick since the early 1900s.
Things a ship's captain might shout.Abracadabra: The word appears in the writings of a Roman medical author around the 200s, who recommended it written on amulets to cure fever.
Things a ship's captain might shout.Howzat: A cricketer's appeal to the umpire, short for 'how is that?', that lets the fielder ask if a batter is out.
Things a ship's captain might shout.Tally-ho: The cry of fox hunters on sighting the fox, and later shouted by RAF pilots, as in the Battle of Britain.
Things a ship's captain might shout.Geronimo: Paratroopers in the US shouted it as they jumped in the 1940s, after a film about the Apache leader.
Things a ship's captain might shout.Eureka: Archimedes allegedly shouted 'I have found it' in the bath after working out volume by displacement.
Things a ship's captain might shout.Bon appétit: French for 'good appetite', said at the start of a meal.

Vehicles that use no fuel.Bicycle: A cyclist is among the most energy-efficient travelers on Earth, using less energy per kilometer than a walker.
Vehicles that use no fuel.Rowboat: Rowing faces backward, so a rower sees where they've been, not where they're going.
Vehicles that use no fuel.Canoe: The word comes from the Caribbean 'kenu', and canoes were the highways of North America's rivers and lakes.
Vehicles that use no fuel.Kayak: Traditional Inuit kayaks were built from sealskin stretched over a driftwood or whalebone frame.
Vehicles that use no fuel.Skateboard: Skateboarding began in 1950s California as 'sidewalk surfing' when surfers wanted something to do on flat days.
Vehicles that use no fuel.Glider: A glider has no engine and stays up by riding rising air; pilots have flown over 3,000 km in a single flight.
Vehicles that use no fuel.Hang glider: Hang gliders fly by shifting body weight, and skilled pilots can stay aloft for hours using thermals.
Vehicles that use no fuel.Sled: Sleds are among the oldest vehicles: runner sleds existed thousands of years before the wheel took off in snowy lands.
Vehicles that use no fuel.Pedalo: A pedalo is a small pedal-powered pleasure boat, a staple of lakes and beaches in Europe.
Vehicles that use no fuel.Unicycle: A unicycle has no gears or brakes, and the pedals are attached directly to the wheel.
Vehicles that use no fuel.Tricycle: A tricycle trades speed for stability, and adult versions are used for deliveries in many cities.
Vehicles that use no fuel.Moped: A moped's name merges 'motor' and 'pedal', because early ones had pedals as well as an engine.
Vehicles that use no fuel.Motorboat: It has a motor, so it needs fuel, even if it looks like a rowboat.
Vehicles that use no fuel.Jet ski: A jet ski is a water scooter, a brand name often used for all personal watercraft, and it burns petrol.
Vehicles that use no fuel.Snowmobile: Snowmobiles use petrol engines, and they were first built as farm tools for snowy regions.
Vehicles that use no fuel.Helicopter: A helicopter's rotors need fuel-burning engines, and no pedal-powered one has ever flown far.
Vehicles that use no fuel.Tractor: Tractors burn diesel and pull farm equipment, though some farms are switching to electric.
Vehicles that use no fuel.Bus: A bus runs on diesel, gas or electricity, and a single full one can replace dozens of cars.
Vehicles that use no fuel.Tuk-tuk: Tuk-tuks are three-wheeled taxis named for the sound of their small engines, and common in Thailand.
Vehicles that use no fuel.Hot air balloon: A hot air balloon burns propane to heat its air, so it does use fuel.
Vehicles that use no fuel.Blimp: A blimp is held up by helium, but its engines still burn fuel to move it.
Vehicles that use no fuel.Quad bike: A quad bike has a petrol engine and four fat wheels for rough terrain.
Vehicles that use no fuel.Go-kart: A go-kart is small, but its little engine still burns petrol, or runs on batteries.
Vehicles that use no fuel.Speedboat: A speedboat's big engines drink fuel fast, sometimes hundreds of liters in an hour at full speed.

Things at a movie theater.Screen: Biggest cinema screens, called IMAX, can be over 20 meters wide, and the very first films had no sound.
Things at a movie theater.Projector: Old film projectors showed 24 frames each second, and each frame is a still picture.
Things at a movie theater.Popcorn: Popcorn became cinema fare during the Depression because it was cheap, and theaters later made more profit from it than from tickets.
Things at a movie theater.Ticket booth: The ticket booth is where tickets are sold, and the first movie theaters, nickelodeons, charged five cents.
Things at a movie theater.Usher: Ushers with flashlights guide moviegoers to seats, and the word comes from the Latin ostiarius, a doorkeeper.
Things at a movie theater.Aisle: Cinema aisles often have little lights along the floor so you can find your seat without disturbing the film.
Things at a movie theater.Trailer: The name 'trailer' stuck because movie previews once trailed after the main feature.
Things at a movie theater.Exit sign: Exit signs glow green in many countries and are required, so you can leave when the lights go out.
Things at a movie theater.Concession stand: The concession stand sells snacks, and the profit margin on soda and popcorn is far higher than on tickets.
Things at a movie theater.3D glasses: 3D glasses work by sending a slightly different image to each eye, and the effect is how your brain judges depth.
Things at a movie theater.Reclining seat: Reclining cinema seats with footrests spread from luxury theaters to ordinary multiplexes in the 2010s.
Things at a movie theater.Altar: An altar belongs in a church, and cinema-goers sometimes treat a movie like a ritual, but it isn't there.
Things at a movie theater.Treadmill: A treadmill is gym equipment, and you wouldn't want one in front of the screen.
Things at a movie theater.Trapeze: A trapeze belongs to a circus, a different kind of show.
Things at a movie theater.Hospital bed: A hospital bed is for patients, and cinemas only have seats.
Things at a movie theater.Bunk bed: A bunk bed is for sleeping, though some people do doze in a movie.
Things at a movie theater.Pitchfork: A pitchfork is a farm tool, and also a name of a music website, but no part of a cinema.
Things at a movie theater.Anvil: An anvil is a blacksmith's tool, and also a cartoon staple, but not a cinema fixture.
Things at a movie theater.Bathtub: Bathtubs go in bathrooms, although in some novelty cinemas viewers sit in them.
Things at a movie theater.Stethoscope: A stethoscope is a doctor's tool, not a cinema item.
Things at a movie theater.Gavel: A gavel belongs in a courtroom, where the drama is real.
Things at a movie theater.Fire pole: Fire poles are for firefighters to slide down fast, in fire stations rather than cinemas.
Things at a movie theater.Kiln: A kiln is a potter's oven, and it's a very hot place unlike a cinema.
Things at a movie theater.Loom: A loom weaves cloth, and it's a textile tool, not a cinema fixture.

Fictional cats.Garfield: Garfield hates Mondays, loves lasagna, and has been called the world's most widely syndicated comic strip.
Fictional cats.Tom: Tom chases Jerry in Hanna-Barbera cartoons, and the pair won seven Academy Awards.
Fictional cats.Sylvester: Sylvester's Looney Tunes catchphrase is 'Sufferin' succotash', and he is perpetually thwarted by Tweety.
Fictional cats.Felix: Felix is among the earliest cartoon stars, popular in the 1920s with a bag of tricks and a long career since.
Fictional cats.Cheshire Cat: The Cheshire Cat in Alice's Adventures in Wonderland fades away until only a grin is left.
Fictional cats.Puss in Boots: Puss in Boots is a clever cat that tricks a king in a 1697 tale, and later Shrek's sidekick.
Fictional cats.Salem: Salem is the wisecracking black cat in Sabrina the Teenage Witch, a witch turned into a cat as punishment.
Fictional cats.Crookshanks: Crookshanks is Hermione's ginger half-Kneazle cat, who sees through Scabbers' disguise.
Fictional cats.Mrs. Norris: Mrs. Norris is the caretaker Filch's cat at Hogwarts, and is petrified by the Basilisk.
Fictional cats.Scratchy: Scratchy is the cat in The Simpsons' Itchy & Scratchy, who always suffers the violence.
Fictional cats.Figaro: Figaro is Geppetto's pet kitten in Pinocchio, who sleeps in a fishbowl with Cleo.
Fictional cats.Duchess: Duchess is the elegant mother cat in Disney's The Aristocats, set in Paris in 1910.
Fictional cats.Top Cat: Top Cat is the leader of the alley cats in New York, with sidekick Benny the Ball, in a 1961 series.
Fictional cats.Odie: Odie is a dog and not a cat; he's Garfield's roommate.
Fictional cats.Snoopy: Snoopy is a beagle, not a cat; his famous rival for his supper dish is a cat next door, and he often imagines himself a flying ace.
Fictional cats.Jerry: Jerry is a mouse, not a cat; the mouse who beats the cat Tom in cartoon after cartoon, and the pair won seven Oscars.
Fictional cats.Tweety: Tweety is a canary, so not a cat; he's chased by Sylvester.
Fictional cats.Toothless: Toothless is a dragon, though he behaves much like a cat and has been compared to one.
Fictional cats.Pikachu: Pikachu is an electric mouse Pokémon, not a cat; Meowth is the cat.
Fictional cats.Stuart Little: Stuart Little is a mouse raised by a human family.
Fictional cats.Speedy Gonzales: Speedy Gonzales is a Mexican mouse, so no cat; he outruns Sylvester.
Fictional cats.Woodstock: Woodstock is Snoopy's yellow bird, not a cat.
Fictional cats.Gizmo: Gizmo is a Mogwai from Gremlins, a furry creature, so he's not a cat.
Fictional cats.Scooby-Doo: Scooby-Doo is a Great Dane and so a dog.

Fictional robots.R2-D2: R2-D2 is the beeping astromech droid of Star Wars, whose sounds were created by sound designer Ben Burtt.
Fictional robots.C-3PO: C-3PO is a protocol droid fluent in over six million forms of communication, and mostly worried.
Fictional robots.WALL-E: WALL-E, a trash-compacting robot, is left alone on Earth, and he falls for EVE in Pixar's 2008 film.
Fictional robots.EVE: EVE is a probe robot sent to find plant life in WALL-E, and her name stands for Extraterrestrial Vegetation Evaluator.
Fictional robots.Bender: Bender Bending Rodríguez is Futurama's foul-mouthed robot, who is powered by alcohol and loves to bend things.
Fictional robots.Baymax: Baymax is an inflatable healthcare robot in Big Hero 6, modeled on soft robotics research.
Fictional robots.Robby the Robot: Robby the Robot debuted in 1956's Forbidden Planet, and later appeared in many other shows.
Fictional robots.Johnny 5: Johnny 5 is the sentient military robot of Short Circuit, who shouts 'Need input!'.
Fictional robots.Iron Giant: The Iron Giant is a huge robot who eats metal, in Brad Bird's 1999 animated film, and chooses to be a hero.
Fictional robots.Rosie the Robot: Rosie the Robot is the Jetsons' sassy robot maid, in a show set in 2062.
Fictional robots.K-9: K-9 is Doctor Who's robot dog, who debuted in 1977, and has a gun in his nose.
Fictional robots.Astro Boy: Astro Boy is a robot boy created by Osamu Tezuka in 1952, and a pillar of manga.
Fictional robots.Chewbacca: Chewbacca is a Wookiee, not a robot; Ben Burtt blended bear, walrus and other animal sounds to make his voice.
Fictional robots.Yoda: Yoda is a Jedi Master of unknown species, not a robot; he is about 900 years old and speaks with odd word order.
E.T. is an alien botanist, not a robot, in Spielberg's 1982 film; the film's ending made countless viewers cry.
Fictional robots.Stitch: Stitch is an alien experiment, not a robot; Experiment 626 is built to be destructive but learns about family in Hawaii.
Fictional robots.Pinocchio: Pinocchio is a wooden puppet that comes to life, not a robot, in a story by Carlo Collodi from 1883; his nose grows when he lies.
Fictional robots.Gizmo: Gizmo is a Mogwai, a furry creature, and not a robot; the Gremlins rule is don't feed him after midnight.
Fictional robots.Kermit: Kermit is a puppet, not a robot; Jim Henson made him from an old green coat of his mother's, and first used him in 1955.
Fictional robots.ALF: ALF is an alien from Melmac, not a robot; the 1986 puppet's name stands for Alien Life Form, and he fancies eating cats.
Fictional robots.Groot: Groot is a tree-like alien, not a robot; his only words are 'I am Groot', and a baby version appears in the Guardians films.
Fictional robots.Mr. Potato Head: Mr. Potato Head is a toy but not a robot, and in 1952 he was the first toy advertised on TV.
Fictional robots.Gollum: Gollum is a creature once like a hobbit, not a robot; the Ring corrupted him over centuries, and Andy Serkis played him with motion capture.
Fictional robots.Shrek: Shrek is an ogre, not a robot; William Steig's picture book inspired the 2001 film, which won the first Oscar for animated feature.

Traditional carols (not pop Christmas so.Silent Night: First performed in 1818 in Austria, reportedly with guitar since the church organ was broken, and now translated into many languages.
Traditional carols (not pop Christmas so.Joy to the World: Isaac Watts wrote the text in 1719 about Christ's reign rather than his birth, yet it is the most-published Christmas hymn.
Traditional carols (not pop Christmas so.O Holy Night: In 1906, Reginald Fessenden is said to have played it on violin in one of the first radio music broadcasts.
Traditional carols (not pop Christmas so.Away in a Manger: Long credited to Martin Luther, it is actually American in origin, first published in the 1880s.
Traditional carols (not pop Christmas so.The First Noel: A Cornish carol published in 1823; 'noel' comes from the Latin for 'birth'.
Traditional carols (not pop Christmas so.Good King Wenceslas: Based on a real 10th-century Duke of Bohemia, though the 1853 lyrics invented the story of the page and snow.
Traditional carols (not pop Christmas so.Adeste Fideles: The Latin original of 'O Come, All Ye Faithful', linked to John Francis Wade in the 1740s.
Traditional carols (not pop Christmas so.Deck the Halls: The tune is a Welsh winter melody from the 1500s, and the 'fa la la' goes back to old Welsh song.
Traditional carols (not pop Christmas so.Coventry Carol: A medieval carol from the 1500s sung in mystery plays about Herod's slaughter, a haunting lullaby.
Traditional carols (not pop Christmas so.We Three Kings: Written in 1857 by Rev. John Henry Hopkins Jr. in Pennsylvania; the Bible never says the Magi were kings or three.
Traditional carols (not pop Christmas so.Ding Dong Merrily: Famous for the long 'Gloria, Hosanna in excelsis' refrain; the tune is from a 16th-century dance book.
Traditional carols (not pop Christmas so.O Christmas Tree: Based on a German song, 'O Tannenbaum', whose original lines were about faithfulness rather than Christmas.
Traditional carols (not pop Christmas so.Let It Snow: Written in 1945 during a Hollywood heat wave by Sammy Cahn and Jule Styne, and never mentions Christmas.
Traditional carols (not pop Christmas so.Frosty the Snowman: A 1950 pop song for Gene Autry, not an old carol.
Traditional carols (not pop Christmas so.Winter Wonderland: A 1934 pop song that never mentions Christmas.
Traditional carols (not pop Christmas so.Sleigh Ride: Composed by Leroy Anderson during a summer heat wave, with lyrics added later, a winter song rather than a carol.
Traditional carols (not pop Christmas so.Run Rudolph Run: Chuck Berry's 1958 rock-and-roll tune, a pop favorite, not a carol.
Traditional carols (not pop Christmas so.White Christmas: Irving Berlin's 1942 song is credited by Guinness as the best-selling single ever.
Traditional carols (not pop Christmas so.Last Christmas: Wham!'s 1984 hit was famously kept off number one by Band Aid's Do They Know It's Christmas?
Traditional carols (not pop Christmas so.Santa Baby: A 1953 pop song, sung by Eartha Kitt, with a flirty list of luxury gifts.
Traditional carols (not pop Christmas so.Feliz Navidad: Jose Feliciano's 1970 hit, built on a single line of Spanish and one of English.
Traditional carols (not pop Christmas so.Blue Christmas: Popularized by Elvis in 1957, it is a country-pop standard, not a traditional carol.
Traditional carols (not pop Christmas so.Mele Kalikimaka: Hawaiian for 'Merry Christmas', a 1949 pop song by R. Alex Anderson, popularized by Bing Crosby.
Traditional carols (not pop Christmas so.Jingle Bell Rock: A 1957 hit by Bobby Helms, a rock-and-roll Christmas song, not a traditional carol.

Typical New Year's resolutions.Lose weight: It is one of the most common resolutions, and studies suggest only a minority of resolutions last the whole year.
Typical New Year's resolutions.Exercise more: Gyms are packed in January, and the rush famously fades by about February.
Typical New Year's resolutions.Quit smoking: Many try it, and research shows that people who set a firm quit date have better odds.
Typical New Year's resolutions.Save money: A top goal, and automatic transfers into savings tend to work better than relying on willpower.
Typical New Year's resolutions.Learn a language: Apps such as Duolingo see big spikes in January, and a few minutes daily beats long, rare sessions.
Typical New Year's resolutions.Read more: It's a popular goal, and a common tip is to aim for just 20 pages a day, which adds up to many books a year.
Typical New Year's resolutions.Eat healthier: Often paired with losing weight, and small swaps tend to last longer than total overhauls.
Typical New Year's resolutions.Drink less: Dry January started as a UK campaign in 2013, and it now has many participants.
Typical New Year's resolutions.Travel more: A popular aim, and it often needs planning of time off early in the year.
Typical New Year's resolutions.Get organized: A resolution many make, and the tidy-up craze rose with Marie Kondo's 2019 series.
Typical New Year's resolutions.Meditate: Mindfulness apps boom each January, and even a few minutes a day is shown to help reduce stress.
Typical New Year's resolutions.Sleep more: Adults usually need seven to nine hours, and sleep is increasingly treated as a goal in its own right.
Typical New Year's resolutions.Eat more junk food: Nobody resolves to do this. Resolutions are goals for self-improvement, so this one is out.
Typical New Year's resolutions.Procrastinate: Ironically, this is what often derails real resolutions, and it is not a resolution anyone makes.
Typical New Year's resolutions.Sleep less: People tend to want more rest, and not less, and so this is not a typical resolution.
Typical New Year's resolutions.Start smoking: The opposite of a standard resolution, and no one resolves to take up a harmful habit.
Typical New Year's resolutions.Spend recklessly: This contradicts the common goal of saving money, so it is not a typical resolution.
Typical New Year's resolutions.Skip the gym: An anti-resolution, since exercise is one of the most common aims of January.
Typical New Year's resolutions.Watch more TV: Few people list this as an aim. If anything, people resolve to cut screen time.
Typical New Year's resolutions.Stay in debt: Paying off debt is a common resolution, and this is the reverse of it.
Typical New Year's resolutions.Drink more soda: The reverse of the usual health goals, where people say they will cut sugar.
Typical New Year's resolutions.Ignore friends: People often resolve to see friends more, so this does not belong.
Typical New Year's resolutions.Stay up late: It runs against the common goal of better sleep, so it is not a typical resolution.
Typical New Year's resolutions.Never exercise: It is the opposite of one of the most common resolutions, to exercise more.
